topics.brief: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties, and transformations of matter. Its scope includes understanding substances, chemical reactions, energy changes, and the development of new materials.

topics.topic: Importance of chemistry in daily life
topics.brief: Chemistry is important in medicines, agriculture, food preservation, cleaning products, fuels, cosmetics, and industrial manufacturing. It helps explain everyday processes such as cooking, digestion, combustion, and rusting.

The major branches include organic chemistry, inorganic chemistry, physical chemistry, analytical chemistry, and biochemistry. Each focuses on different aspects of substances, including carbon compounds, inorganic materials, energy changes, chemical analysis, and chemical processes in living organisms.

Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It can be classified by physical state as solid, liquid, or gas, and by composition as a pure substance or mixture. Pure substances include elements and compounds.

An element contains one type of atom and cannot be broken down chemically into simpler substances. A compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. A mixture contains substances physically combined in variable proportions and can generally be separated by physical methods.

Physical properties can be observed without changing a substance's chemical identity, such as density, colour, melting point, and boiling point. Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts to form new substances, such as flammability, acidity, and reactivity with oxygen.

A physical change alters a substance's state, shape, or appearance without changing its chemical identity, such as melting ice. A chemical change produces one or more new substances, as in rusting iron, burning wood, or reacting an acid with a base.

An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity. A molecule consists of two or more atoms chemically bonded together. An ion is an electrically charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.

Atomic mass is the mass of an atom, commonly expressed in unified atomic mass units (u). Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms present in a molecule. For example, the molecular mass of water is approximately 18 u.

Relative atomic mass (Ar) is the weighted average mass of atoms of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It accounts for the natural abundances of the element's isotopes and has no unit.

Relative molecular mass (Mr) is the ratio of the average mass of a molecule to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It is calculated by adding the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula and has no unit.

The mole is the SI unit for the amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified elementary entities, such as atoms, molecules, or ions. The mole concept connects microscopic particles with measurable quantities of substances.

The Avogadro constant is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. It specifies the number of elementary entities in one mole of a substance and is used to convert between the amount of substance and the number of particles.

Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, usually expressed in grams per mole (g mol⁻¹). It is numerically equal to the relative atomic, molecular, or formula mass when expressed in the corresponding molar-mass units.

Molar volume is the volume occupied by one mole of a gas at a specified temperature and pressure. For an ideal gas, it depends on these conditions; at 273.15 K and 1 atm, one mole occupies approximately 22.4 L.

A chemical formula represents the elements in a substance and the relative number of their atoms or ions. Molecular formulae show the actual numbers of atoms in molecules, while empirical formulae show the simplest whole-number ratio. Ionic compounds are represented by formula units.

A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using symbols and formulae. Reactants appear on the left and products on the right. State symbols and reaction conditions may also be included to describe how the reaction occurs.

Balancing a chemical equation ensures that the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides, consistent with conservation of mass. This is done by adjusting coefficients in front of chemical formulae without changing their subscripts.

The International System of Units provides standardized measurements for chemical quantities. Important units include the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K), mole (mol), and ampere (A). Derived units such as pascal, joule, and cubic metre are also used in chemistry.

Scientific notation expresses very large or small numbers as a coefficient multiplied by a power of ten. Significant figures indicate the meaningful precision of a measurement. Correct use of both helps communicate chemical measurements and calculation results accurately.

The laws of chemical combination describe quantitative relationships between substances in chemical reactions. Important laws include conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions, gaseous volume relationships, and Avogadro's law.

The law of conservation of mass states that mass is conserved during an ordinary chemical reaction in a closed system. The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products because atoms are rearranged rather than created or destroyed.

The law of definite proportions states that a pure chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass. For example, pure water contains hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of approximately 1:8.

The law of multiple proportions states that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios. For example, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide contain oxygen in a 1:2 mass ratio for a fixed mass of carbon.

Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes states that reacting gases and gaseous products, measured at the same temperature and pressure, have volumes in simple whole-number ratios. For example, two volumes of hydrogen react with one volume of oxygen to form two volumes of gaseous water under suitable conditions.

Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Consequently, the volume of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the number of moles when temperature and pressure remain constant.

Dalton's atomic theory proposed that matter consists of atoms and that compounds form when atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios. It helped explain the laws of chemical combination. Modern evidence shows that atoms contain subatomic particles and that atoms of the same element can have different masses because of isotopes.

Mole-mass-particle calculations connect the amount of substance with its mass and number of particles. The relationships are n = m/M and N = nNA, where n is the amount in moles, m is mass, M is molar mass, N is the number of particles, and NA is the Avogadro constant.

For an ideal gas, the amount of substance, pressure, volume, and temperature are related by PV = nRT. At constant temperature and pressure, gas volume is proportional to the number of moles. Calculations must use the appropriate molar volume or gas constant for the stated conditions.

Percentage composition gives the percentage by mass contributed by each element in a compound. It is calculated by dividing the total mass of the element in one mole of the compound by the compound's molar mass and multiplying by 100.

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. It can be determined from percentage composition or elemental masses by converting each amount to moles and simplifying the mole ratio.

The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule. It is obtained by multiplying the empirical formula by an integer, calculated from the ratio of the compound's molar mass to its empirical formula mass.

Chemical equation calculations use a balanced equation to determine the quantities of reactants consumed and products formed. The coefficients give mole ratios, which can be converted into masses, particle numbers, or gas volumes using the relevant chemical relationships.

The limiting reagent is the reactant that is consumed first in a chemical reaction. It determines the maximum amount of product that can form. To identify it, compare the available moles of each reactant with the mole ratios required by the balanced equation.

An excess reagent is a reactant supplied in a greater amount than required by the balanced chemical equation. Some of it remains after the limiting reagent has been completely consumed. Its remaining amount can be calculated by subtracting the amount that reacted from the initial amount.

Theoretical yield is the maximum amount of product predicted by stoichiometric calculations when the limiting reagent reacts completely according to the balanced equation. It assumes ideal reaction conditions and no product loss.

Actual yield is the quantity of product obtained experimentally from a chemical reaction. It may be lower than the theoretical yield because of incomplete reactions, side reactions, or losses during separation and purification.

Percentage yield compares the actual amount of product obtained with the theoretical maximum. It is calculated as percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100. It is used to evaluate the efficiency of a chemical process.

Purity calculations determine the proportion of a sample that consists of the desired substance. Percentage purity is calculated as (mass of pure substance / total mass of sample) × 100. Impurities must be accounted for when determining the amount available for a reaction.

Concentration expresses the amount of solute present in a specified amount of solution or solvent. Molar concentration is calculated as c = n/V, where n is the amount of solute in moles and V is the solution volume in litres. Other forms include mass concentration, percentage concentration, and parts per million.

Gas stoichiometry uses balanced chemical equations together with gas laws to calculate the quantities of gaseous reactants and products. Gas volumes can be compared directly using mole ratios when all gases are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

Atomic models developed as experimental evidence revealed the internal structure of atoms. Dalton described atoms as basic units of matter, Thomson discovered electrons, Rutherford established the nuclear model, and Bohr introduced quantized electron energy levels. Modern quantum mechanics describes electrons using orbitals and probability distributions.

J. J. Thomson identified the electron through experiments with cathode rays in discharge tubes. He showed that cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles present in atoms of different substances, demonstrating that atoms are divisible.

The proton is a positively charged subatomic particle found in the atomic nucleus. Its identification followed investigations of positive rays and nuclear structure. The number of protons in an atom determines its atomic number and identifies the element.

James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 through experiments involving radiation from beryllium. Neutrons have no electric charge and are found in the nuclei of most atoms. They contribute to atomic mass and help influence nuclear stability.

Thomson proposed that an atom was a positively charged sphere containing embedded electrons, making the atom electrically neutral overall. This model incorporated the newly discovered electron but could not explain the results of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment.

Rutherford's nuclear model was based on alpha-particle scattering experiments using thin gold foil. It proposed that most of an atom is empty space and that nearly all its positive charge and mass are concentrated in a small, dense nucleus, with electrons occupying the surrounding region.

Rutherford's model could not explain why orbiting electrons do not continuously lose energy and fall into the nucleus according to classical physics. It also failed to explain the discrete line spectra observed in atoms.

Bohr proposed that electrons occupy specific permitted energy levels around the nucleus. Electrons absorb or emit energy when moving between these levels. His model successfully explained the hydrogen spectrum but was less successful for atoms containing multiple electrons.

Bohr's model explains hydrogen-like species well but does not accurately describe the spectra and electronic behaviour of most multi-electron atoms. It also assumes definite electron orbits, which are inconsistent with the modern quantum-mechanical description of electrons.

Electromagnetic radiation consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that carry energy through space. It includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. In a vacuum, all electromagnetic radiation travels at approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

Wavelength is the distance between successive wave peaks, while frequency is the number of wave cycles passing a point each second. Wave speed is given by c = λν for electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum, where c is the speed of light, λ is wavelength, and ν is frequency.

Planck's quantum theory states that electromagnetic energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets called quanta. The energy of a photon is E = hν, where h is Planck's constant and ν is frequency. This idea helped explain blackbody radiation and the quantized nature of atomic energy.

The photoelectric effect occurs when light of sufficiently high frequency strikes a material and causes electrons to be emitted. It supports the particle nature of light because electron emission depends on photon energy, which is proportional to frequency, rather than simply on light intensity.

Atomic spectra are patterns of wavelengths emitted or absorbed by atoms. Electrons can occupy only particular energy states, so transitions between these states involve specific energy differences. Each element therefore has a characteristic spectrum that can help identify it.

The hydrogen emission spectrum consists of discrete lines produced when excited electrons transition from higher to lower energy levels. The Balmer series includes visible lines, while the Lyman and Paschen series lie mainly in the ultraviolet and infrared regions, respectively.

Energy levels are allowed energy states that electrons can occupy in atoms. Electrons absorb energy to move to higher levels and release energy when returning to lower levels. The energy difference determines the frequency or wavelength of the absorbed or emitted radiation.

De Broglie proposed that particles such as electrons have wave-like properties. The associated wavelength is given by λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant and p is the particle's momentum. This hypothesis contributed to the development of quantum mechanics.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that the position and momentum of a particle cannot both be known with unlimited precision at the same time. This is an inherent feature of quantum systems rather than simply a limitation of measuring instruments.

Quantum numbers describe the allowed states of electrons in atoms. The four quantum numbers are principal, azimuthal, magnetic, and spin quantum numbers. Together, they describe an electron's energy level, orbital type, orbital orientation, and spin state.

The principal quantum number, n, identifies the main electron shell and is a positive integer such as 1, 2, or 3. It is related to the energy and approximate size of an orbital, particularly in hydrogen-like atoms.

The azimuthal quantum number, l, identifies the subshell and the general shape of an orbital. For a given principal quantum number n, l ranges from 0 to n − 1. The values 0, 1, 2, and 3 correspond to s, p, d, and f subshells.

The magnetic quantum number, ml, describes the orientation of an orbital within a subshell. For a given l, it can take integer values from −l to +l, including zero. These values determine the number of orbitals in the subshell.

The spin quantum number describes an electron's intrinsic angular momentum. Its permitted values are +1/2 and −1/2. Two electrons occupying the same orbital must have opposite spin quantum numbers according to the Pauli exclusion principle.

An atomic orbital is a quantum-mechanical description of a region where an electron is likely to be found. Orbitals have characteristic energies, shapes, and orientations. Each orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins.

topics.topic: Shapes of s, p and d orbitals
topics.brief: An s orbital is approximately spherical, while p orbitals generally have two lobes oriented along three perpendicular axes. d orbitals have more complex shapes, most commonly four-lobed forms, with the dz² orbital having a different shape. These shapes represent electron probability distributions.

The Aufbau principle states that electrons generally occupy available orbitals in order of increasing energy. It helps predict ground-state electronic configurations, although some transition elements show exceptions because orbital energies can be very close.

The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers. Consequently, an orbital can contain at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.

Hund's rule states that electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly with parallel spins before pairing occurs. This arrangement generally lowers electron-electron repulsion and produces a more stable electronic configuration.

Electronic configuration describes how electrons are distributed among shells, subshells, and orbitals in an atom. It is determined using energy-ordering rules, the Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund's rule. Electronic configuration helps explain chemical properties and periodic trends.

The electronic configuration of an ion is obtained by adding electrons to form anions or removing electrons to form cations. For transition-metal cations, electrons are generally removed from the outermost ns subshell before the (n − 1)d subshell, even though the d subshell may be filled earlier.

chapters.chapterName: Classification of Elements and Periodic Table

topics.topic: Historical development of the periodic table
topics.brief: The periodic table developed through attempts to organize elements according to their properties and atomic masses. Contributions from scientists such as Döbereiner, Newlands, and Mendeleev led to the modern arrangement based on atomic number and recurring chemical properties.

Döbereiner grouped certain elements into triads of three with similar chemical properties. In some triads, the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the average of the other two. The system was useful but applied to only a limited number of elements.

Newlands proposed that when elements were arranged in increasing order of atomic mass, every eighth element showed similar properties. This pattern, called the law of octaves, worked reasonably well for some lighter elements but failed for many heavier elements.

Mendeleev arranged elements mainly by increasing atomic mass and grouped elements with similar chemical properties. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted some of their properties. The discovery of these elements supported the usefulness of his periodic table.

The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Repeating patterns arise because similar outer-electron configurations recur at regular intervals as atomic number increases.

The modern periodic table arranges elements in increasing order of atomic number. It contains seven periods and eighteen groups, with elements placed according to their electronic configurations and recurring chemical properties.

Periods are horizontal rows in the periodic table, while groups are vertical columns. For many main-group elements, the period indicates the highest occupied principal shell and the group relates to the number of valence electrons. Elements in the same group often have similar chemical properties.

The periodic table is divided into s, p, d, and f blocks according to the subshell being filled by the differentiating electron. The s- and p-blocks contain the main-group elements, the d-block contains the transition elements, and the f-block contains the lanthanoids and actinoids.

Periodic trends arise from repeating patterns in electronic configuration as atomic number increases. The number of occupied shells, effective nuclear charge, shielding, and valence-electron arrangement influence atomic size, ionisation energy, electron affinity, and chemical reactivity.

Atomic radius is a measure of atomic size, defined using distances between nuclei under specified bonding conditions. It generally decreases across a period as effective nuclear charge increases and tends to increase down a group as additional electron shells are occupied.

Ionic radius describes the effective size of an ion in a crystal or ionic environment. Cations are generally smaller than their parent atoms because they lose electrons, while anions are generally larger because they gain electrons. In an isoelectronic series, radius usually decreases as nuclear charge increases.

Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom or ion. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group, although subshell structure and electron pairing produce exceptions.

Electron affinity describes the energy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom. The process is often exothermic for many nonmetals, but values vary because of electronic configuration and electron-electron repulsion. Sign conventions should be checked when comparing tabulated values.

Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a chemical bond to attract shared electrons. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. Differences in electronegativity help predict bond polarity and the distribution of electron density in molecules.

Valency describes an element's combining capacity, while oxidation state is a formal charge assigned to an atom using agreed electron-allocation rules. Many elements have characteristic valencies or oxidation states, but some, especially transition elements, exhibit several possible oxidation states.

Metallic character refers to the tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions, while non-metallic character is associated with electron attraction and electron sharing or gain. Metallic character generally increases down a group and decreases across a period.

Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally decreases, ionisation energy and electronegativity generally increase, and metallic character decreases. These trends arise mainly from increasing nuclear charge while electrons are added to the same principal shell, with some exceptions.

Down a group, atomic and ionic radii generally increase because additional electron shells are occupied. Ionisation energy and electronegativity generally decrease, while metallic character often increases. These patterns can show exceptions because of shielding and electronic structure.

Representative elements are the s- and p-block elements. Their chemical properties are strongly influenced by their valence-electron configurations, which explain patterns in bonding, reactivity, oxidation states, and the formation of ions and compounds within groups and periods.

topics.topic: Relationship between position and electronic configuration
topics.brief: An element's position in the periodic table is related to its electronic configuration. The period generally corresponds to the highest occupied principal energy level, while the block identifies the subshell being filled. Valence-electron arrangements help explain group placement and chemical behaviour.

Chemical bonding involves attractive interactions that hold atoms or ions together in substances. Ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding arise from different patterns of electron transfer, sharing, or delocalisation. Bonding influences the stability, structure, and properties of materials.

The octet rule states that many atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve eight electrons in their valence shell, resembling a noble-gas configuration. It is a useful introductory guide for predicting bonding, especially in many main-group compounds.

The octet rule does not explain every stable molecule. Some compounds have incomplete octets, such as BF3; odd numbers of electrons, such as NO; or expanded valence-shell descriptions, such as SF6 in conventional introductory models. It also does not independently predict molecular shape or bond strength.

Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It commonly forms when electron transfer produces cations and anions, which arrange into a crystal lattice. Ionic bonding is associated with compounds such as sodium chloride.

Ionic compounds form when atoms transfer electrons to produce positive and negative ions that attract one another. The resulting ions arrange into a lattice, and the formula represents the simplest ratio that gives overall electrical neutrality.

Lattice energy describes the energy change associated with forming or separating an ionic crystal from gaseous ions. Its numerical sign depends on the convention used. Its magnitude generally increases with higher ionic charges and smaller ionic radii, reflecting stronger electrostatic attraction.

Covalent bonding occurs when atoms share pairs of electrons. It is common between nonmetal atoms and can form discrete molecules or extended covalent networks. The number and distribution of shared electron pairs influence bond strength, length, and molecular geometry.

A single covalent bond contains one shared electron pair, a double bond contains two shared pairs, and a triple bond contains three. In comparable bonds between the same atoms, higher bond order generally corresponds to shorter and stronger bonds.

A coordinate covalent bond forms when both electrons in a shared pair are donated by the same atom. The donor provides a lone pair to an electron-deficient acceptor. For example, ammonia can donate a lone pair to a hydrogen ion to form ammonium.

Lewis structures represent valence electrons as dots and covalent bonds as shared pairs, often shown by lines. They help identify bonding pairs, lone pairs, and approximate connectivity in molecules and polyatomic ions.

Formal charge is an accounting charge assigned to an atom in a Lewis structure. It is calculated as valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons. Formal charges help compare possible structures but are not necessarily the actual charges on atoms.

Resonance occurs when a molecule or ion cannot be adequately represented by a single Lewis structure. Several valid structures differ in electron placement but retain the same atomic arrangement. The actual structure is a resonance hybrid, with electron density delocalized across the relevant atoms.

Bond polarity arises when bonded atoms attract shared electrons unequally. This creates partial negative and partial positive regions in the bond. Whether an entire molecule is polar depends on both bond polarities and molecular geometry.

Electronegativity differences help estimate whether a bond is predominantly covalent or has substantial ionic character. Similar electronegativities favour more equal sharing, while larger differences produce greater bond polarity. The distinction is a continuum rather than an absolute division.

Bond length is the average equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. It depends on atomic size, bond order, and the chemical environment. For comparable atoms, triple bonds are generally shorter than double bonds, which are generally shorter than single bonds.

Bond angle is the angle between two bonds that meet at a central atom. It is influenced by electron-pair repulsion, hybridisation, and the surrounding atoms. Bond angles help describe molecular geometry and can affect molecular polarity.

Bond enthalpy is the enthalpy required to break a specified covalent bond in the gaseous state. Average bond enthalpies are used to estimate reaction enthalpy by comparing the energy needed to break bonds with the energy released when new bonds form.

topics.topic: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory
topics.brief: Valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts molecular shapes by assuming that electron domains around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. Lone pairs generally repel more strongly than bonding pairs, which can alter bond angles.

Molecular shape describes the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms. Common shapes include linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, and bent. The shape depends on the number of bonding and nonbonding electron domains around the central atom.

Hybridisation is a model in which atomic orbitals on the same atom combine to form hybrid orbitals with particular orientations. It is commonly used to explain molecular geometry and bonding in introductory chemistry. Examples include sp, sp2, and sp3 hybridisation.

In the sp hybridisation model, one s orbital combines with one p orbital to form two sp hybrid orbitals. These orbitals point in opposite directions, giving a linear arrangement with an ideal angle of 180 degrees. Two unhybridised p orbitals remain available for pi bonding.

In the sp2 hybridisation model, one s orbital combines with two p orbitals to form three sp2 hybrid orbitals. They lie in a plane with ideal angles of approximately 120 degrees. One unhybridised p orbital remains and can participate in pi bonding.

In the sp3 hybridisation model, one s orbital combines with three p orbitals to form four sp3 hybrid orbitals. Their ideal arrangement is tetrahedral, with angles of approximately 109.5 degrees. Lone pairs can modify the observed molecular shape and bond angles.

Molecular orbital theory describes electrons as occupying orbitals spread over an entire molecule rather than belonging exclusively to individual bonds. Atomic orbitals combine to form molecular orbitals that may be bonding, antibonding, or nonbonding. The theory helps explain bond order and magnetic properties.

Bonding molecular orbitals are formed by constructive combination of atomic orbitals and have lower energy than the contributing orbitals. Antibonding orbitals arise from destructive combination, have higher energy, and are marked with an asterisk. Electron occupancy of both types affects molecular stability.

In elementary molecular orbital theory, bond order is calculated as one-half the difference between the number of bonding electrons and antibonding electrons. A higher positive bond order generally indicates a stronger, shorter bond, while a bond order of zero indicates no net bond in the simple model.

Hydrogen bonding is an attraction involving hydrogen covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, commonly nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, and a suitable electron-rich site. It can occur between molecules or within a molecule and helps explain water's unusual properties and the structures of biological molecules.

Intermolecular forces are attractions between separate molecules or particles. They include London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole attractions, and hydrogen bonding. These forces influence boiling points, melting points, viscosity, surface tension, and solubility.

topics.topic: Properties of ionic and covalent compounds
topics.brief: Ionic compounds commonly have high melting points and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water because their ions can move. Molecular covalent substances often have lower melting and boiling points and generally do not conduct electricity, although exceptions occur. Giant covalent structures, such as diamond, can have very high melting points.

Oxidation and reduction are paired processes in which electrons are transferred or oxidation states change. Oxidation involves electron loss or an increase in oxidation number, while reduction involves electron gain or a decrease in oxidation number. Both occur together in a redox reaction.

An oxidising agent causes another substance to be oxidised by accepting electrons from it. The oxidising agent itself is reduced. Common examples include oxygen, chlorine, and potassium permanganate under suitable reaction conditions.

A reducing agent causes another substance to be reduced by donating electrons or otherwise supplying reducing equivalents. The reducing agent itself is oxidised. Examples include hydrogen, carbon monoxide, and certain reactive metals.

Oxidation number is a formal charge assigned to an atom using agreed rules for allocating bonding electrons. It helps track electron transfer in redox reactions. An increase indicates oxidation, while a decrease indicates reduction.

An element in its standard elemental form has oxidation number zero, and a monatomic ion has an oxidation number equal to its charge. Oxygen is usually −2 and hydrogen usually +1 when bonded to nonmetals, with important exceptions. The sum of oxidation numbers equals the total charge of the species.

topics.topic: Oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer
topics.brief: In electron-transfer terms, oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons. For example, when zinc forms zinc ions, it loses electrons, while copper ions gain electrons to form copper metal. The electrons lost by one species are gained by another.

topics.topic: Oxidation and reduction in terms of oxidation number
topics.brief: Oxidation and reduction can be identified by tracking oxidation-number changes. An increase in oxidation number indicates oxidation, while a decrease indicates reduction. This method is useful even when electron transfer is not obvious from the chemical equation.

A reaction is classified as redox when at least one element increases its oxidation number and another decreases its oxidation number. Identifying these changes helps distinguish redox reactions from reactions such as many acid-base neutralisations and precipitation reactions.

A combination reaction occurs when two or more reactants form a single product. Some combination reactions are redox reactions when oxidation numbers change, such as the reaction of magnesium with oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

A decomposition reaction occurs when one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. Decomposition can be caused by heat, light, or electricity. Some decomposition reactions involve oxidation-number changes and are therefore redox reactions.

A displacement reaction occurs when one element replaces another element in a compound. Many such reactions are redox reactions because electrons are transferred between the reacting species. For example, zinc can displace copper from a copper salt solution.

A disproportionation reaction occurs when the same element in one reactant is simultaneously oxidised and reduced to form products with different oxidation states. For example, hydrogen peroxide can decompose to form water and oxygen, with oxygen undergoing both reduction and oxidation.

Balancing redox equations ensures that both atoms and electrical charge are conserved. Common approaches include the oxidation-number method and the ion-electron method. The appropriate method depends on the reaction and whether it occurs in acidic or basic solution.

The oxidation-number method balances a redox equation by identifying changes in oxidation states and adjusting coefficients so that the total increase and decrease in oxidation number are equal. Remaining atoms, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge are then balanced as required by the medium.

The ion-electron method separates a redox reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions. Each half-reaction is balanced for atoms and charge, using electrons and, where appropriate, H2O, H+, or OH−. The half-reactions are then combined and simplified.

Redox reactions occur in combustion, respiration, photosynthesis, corrosion, bleaching, and metal extraction. They are also essential in batteries and electrochemical cells, where electron transfer can be used to generate electrical energy.

chapters.chapterName: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids

topics.brief: Matter commonly exists as solids, liquids, and gases, which differ in particle arrangement, motion, and intermolecular forces. Solids maintain a definite shape, liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container, and gases expand to fill their container.

Intermolecular forces are attractions between particles that influence the physical properties of substances. They include dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding. Stronger intermolecular attractions generally lead to higher boiling points and greater resistance to flow.

The kinetic molecular theory explains gas behaviour by modelling particles as being in continuous random motion with negligible volume and negligible intermolecular attractions in an ideal gas. Collisions are elastic, and average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature.

Gases have no fixed shape or volume and are highly compressible. Their particles move rapidly and randomly, filling the available space. Pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas are related through the gas laws.

Boyle's law states that for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume. The relationship is P1V1 = P2V2. Increasing pressure therefore decreases the gas volume when temperature remains constant.

Charles's law states that the volume of a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. The relationship is V1/T1 = V2/T2, with temperatures expressed in kelvin.

The pressure law states that the pressure of a fixed amount of gas at constant volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. It can be written as P1/T1 = P2/T2, where temperature is measured in kelvin.

Avogadro's law states that the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the amount of gas in moles when temperature and pressure are constant. Equal volumes of ideal gases under the same conditions contain equal numbers of molecules.

The combined gas law relates pressure, volume, and absolute temperature for a fixed amount of gas. It is expressed as P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2. It combines Boyle's, Charles's, and pressure-law relationships.

The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is amount in moles, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. It approximates gas behaviour well under many conditions, especially at relatively low pressure and high temperature.

The universal gas constant R relates pressure, volume, temperature, and amount in the ideal gas equation. Its value is approximately 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ or 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, depending on the units used.

Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases. A gas's partial pressure is the pressure it would exert if it alone occupied the container at the same temperature.

Graham's law states that, under the same conditions, the rate of diffusion or effusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass. Lighter gases generally diffuse or effuse faster than heavier gases.

Diffusion is the spreading and mixing of particles due to random motion. Effusion is the escape of gas particles through a tiny opening. Both processes depend on particle motion, temperature, and molar mass.

The average translational kinetic energy of ideal gas particles depends only on absolute temperature. Per molecule, it is proportional to (3/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant. At the same temperature, different ideal gases have the same average translational kinetic energy.

Root mean square speed is a measure of the typical speed of gas particles calculated from the square root of the mean of their squared speeds. For an ideal gas, it is given by urms = √(3RT/M), where M is molar mass in kg mol⁻¹.

Real gases differ from ideal gases because their particles occupy finite volumes and experience intermolecular attractions. These effects become especially important at high pressure and low temperature. Many gases behave approximately ideally at low pressure and high temperature.

Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour when particle volume and intermolecular forces cannot be neglected. Deviations are often substantial near condensation conditions and at high pressures. The compressibility factor can be used to describe how a real gas differs from the ideal gas model.

The van der Waals equation modifies the ideal gas equation to account approximately for molecular attractions and finite particle volume. It is commonly written as (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, where a represents attraction effects and b represents excluded volume.

Liquefaction converts a gas into a liquid by removing heat and/or increasing pressure under suitable conditions. A gas can be liquefied by pressure alone only when its temperature is below its critical temperature. Industrial methods often use compression, cooling, and expansion.

Critical temperature is the highest temperature at which a substance can be liquefied by applying pressure. Critical pressure is the pressure required to reach the critical point at the critical temperature. Above the critical point, liquid and gas phases are not distinct.

Liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container. Their particles remain close together while moving past one another. Intermolecular forces give liquids properties such as viscosity, surface tension, and relatively low compressibility.

Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid or solid in a closed system. It increases with temperature because more particles gain enough energy to enter the vapour phase. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

Surface tension is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid per unit area, or equivalently the force per unit length under appropriate conditions. It results from cohesive forces between liquid particles and explains phenomena such as droplet formation and capillary effects.

Viscosity measures a fluid's resistance to flow. In liquids, it is influenced by intermolecular attractions, molecular shape, and temperature. For most liquids, viscosity decreases as temperature increases because particles can move past one another more easily.

A reversible reaction can proceed in both forward and reverse directions under suitable conditions. An irreversible reaction proceeds predominantly in one direction under the stated conditions. Reversible reactions can establish dynamic equilibrium in a closed system.

Dynamic equilibrium occurs in a reversible reaction when the forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. The concentrations of reactants and products then remain constant over time, although both reactions continue at the molecular level.

Chemical equilibrium is dynamic and is established in a closed system under suitable conditions. At equilibrium, forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and macroscopic properties remain constant. Reactant and product concentrations are not necessarily equal.

The law of mass action states that, at a given temperature, the equilibrium relationship for a reaction can be expressed using the activities of reactants and products. In dilute solutions and introductory calculations, concentrations are commonly used to formulate the equilibrium constant.

The equilibrium constant expresses the ratio of product activities to reactant activities at equilibrium, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient. Its value depends on temperature and indicates whether products or reactants are favoured at equilibrium, but it does not indicate how fast equilibrium is reached.

topics.topic: Equilibrium constant in terms of concentration
topics.brief: For a reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the concentration equilibrium constant is written Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b), using equilibrium concentrations. Pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the expression.

topics.topic: Equilibrium constant in terms of partial pressure
topics.brief: For gaseous equilibria, Kp is expressed using the equilibrium partial pressures of gaseous products and reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient. Pure solids and liquids are excluded from the expression.

For an ideal-gas reaction, Kp and Kc are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is the total stoichiometric amount of gaseous products minus that of gaseous reactants. The relation assumes consistent units and standard chemistry conventions.

The reaction quotient Q has the same mathematical form as the equilibrium constant but uses the current, not necessarily equilibrium, concentrations or partial pressures. Comparing Q with K indicates the direction in which a reaction must proceed to reach equilibrium under the given conditions.

Homogeneous equilibrium occurs when all reactants and products are in the same physical phase. For example, a reaction involving only gases can establish a homogeneous gaseous equilibrium. Equilibrium expressions include the relevant species according to their activities or concentrations.

Heterogeneous equilibrium involves reactants or products in different physical phases. The activities of pure solids and pure liquids are treated as constant and are omitted from the equilibrium constant expression, while gaseous or dissolved species are included.

Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, the system shifts in a direction that partially opposes the disturbance. The principle helps predict equilibrium shifts but does not replace quantitative calculations.

Changing the concentration of a reactant or product disturbs equilibrium and causes the reaction to shift in a direction that tends to oppose the change. Adding a reactant generally favours its consumption, while removing a product generally favours further product formation. The equilibrium constant remains unchanged if temperature is constant.

topics.topic: Effect of pressure and volume on equilibrium
topics.brief: For gaseous equilibria, increasing pressure by decreasing volume generally favours the side with fewer moles of gas, while decreasing pressure favours the side with more gaseous moles. If both sides have equal total gaseous stoichiometric amounts, a pressure change may not shift the equilibrium.

Temperature changes affect the equilibrium constant and can shift the equilibrium position. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, while decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction. Unlike concentration or pressure changes, temperature changes alter the value of the equilibrium constant.

A catalyst increases the rates of both forward and reverse reactions by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. It helps the system reach equilibrium faster but does not change the equilibrium constant or the final equilibrium composition at a fixed temperature.

Chemical equilibrium principles help optimize industrial processes by selecting suitable temperatures, pressures, and reactant concentrations. For example, the Haber process produces ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, while the Contact process produces sulfur trioxide as part of sulfuric acid manufacture. Industrial conditions balance equilibrium yield, reaction rate, cost, and safety.

Equilibrium calculations use balanced equations, initial concentrations or pressures, and equilibrium constants to determine unknown equilibrium quantities. An ICE table—initial, change, equilibrium—can organize the calculation by expressing how reactant and product amounts change as the system approaches equilibrium.

Non-metals are elements that generally lack metallic properties. They are often poor conductors of heat and electricity, may exist as solids, liquids, or gases, and tend to gain or share electrons during chemical reactions.

Non-metals occur naturally in the atmosphere, oceans, Earth's crust, and living organisms. Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, sulphur, phosphorus, and halogens occur in different forms, including free elements and chemical compounds.
Hydrogen is the lightest element and has the atomic number 1. It occurs mainly in compounds such as water and hydrocarbons and exists as a colourless, odourless, highly combustible diatomic gas (H₂).

Hydrogen can be prepared in the laboratory by reacting suitable metals with dilute acids or water under appropriate conditions. It is a light, combustible gas that reacts with oxygen to form water and acts as a reducing agent in some reactions.

Hydrides are binary compounds of hydrogen with other elements. They are commonly classified as ionic or saline hydrides, covalent or molecular hydrides, and metallic or interstitial hydrides according to their bonding and properties.

Water (H₂O) is a polar molecule with a bent shape and an H–O–H bond angle of approximately 104.5°. Hydrogen bonding between water molecules contributes to its relatively high boiling point, surface tension, and ability to dissolve many substances.

Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions that react with soap to form scum and reduce lather. Soft water contains little or no hardness-causing ions and forms lather more readily with soap.

Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is a pale blue liquid in its pure form and is commonly used as an aqueous solution. It acts as an oxidising agent and, under some conditions, a reducing agent, and decomposes into water and oxygen.

Oxygen (O₂) is a colourless, odourless gas that supports combustion and is essential for aerobic respiration. In the laboratory, it can be prepared by decomposing suitable oxygen-containing compounds, such as hydrogen peroxide, using appropriate conditions.

Oxides are binary compounds of oxygen with another element. Based on their acid-base behaviour, they are classified as acidic, basic, amphoteric, or neutral oxides; they may also be grouped as peroxides and superoxides according to their oxygen species.

Ozone (O₃) is a pale blue, reactive form of oxygen with a distinctive sharp smell. It can be produced when oxygen is subjected to electrical discharge or ultraviolet radiation and is a strong oxidising agent.

The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, helping protect living organisms. Certain ozone-depleting substances can reduce its concentration, increasing the amount of damaging UV radiation reaching Earth's surface.

Nitrogen is a colourless, odourless gas that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere by volume. Molecular nitrogen (N₂) is relatively unreactive at ordinary temperatures because of the strong triple bond between its atoms.

Ammonia (NH₃) is a colourless gas with a pungent smell that dissolves readily in water and behaves as a weak base. Industrially, it is produced by the Haber process, in which nitrogen reacts with hydrogen under suitable temperature, pressure, and catalytic conditions.

Nitric acid (HNO₃) is a strong acid and a powerful oxidising agent. It is manufactured industrially by the Ostwald process, which involves the catalytic oxidation of ammonia followed by further reactions to produce nitric acid.

Phosphorus is a reactive non-metal that exists in several structural forms called allotropes. The main allotropes studied are white phosphorus, red phosphorus, and black phosphorus, which differ in structure, stability, reactivity, and physical properties.

Phosphine (PH₃) is a colourless, highly toxic gas with a weakly basic character. Important phosphorus compounds include phosphates, phosphoric acid, phosphorus oxides, and phosphorus halides, which have applications in fertilisers and chemical manufacturing.

Sulphur is a yellow non-metal that occurs in nature both in elemental form and in compounds. Its common allotropes include rhombic sulphur and monoclinic sulphur, which differ in crystal structure and stability under different temperature conditions.

Sulphur dioxide (SO₂) is a colourless gas with a pungent, choking smell. It dissolves in water, can act as a reducing agent, and is an important air pollutant associated with the combustion of sulphur-containing fuels and the formation of acid rain.

Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) is a strong, diprotic acid widely used in industrial processes. It is manufactured by the Contact process and has important dehydrating and oxidising properties, particularly when concentrated.

Halogens are Group 17 elements, including fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, and astatine. They generally exist as diatomic molecules, are reactive non-metals, and tend to gain one electron to form halide ions.

Hydrogen halides are compounds formed between hydrogen and halogens, such as HF, HCl, HBr, and HI. They are covalent molecules, and their aqueous solutions form hydrohalic acids whose acid strengths generally increase from HF to HI.

Chlorine (Cl₂) is a greenish-yellow, toxic gas with a strong smell and powerful oxidising properties. Its important compounds include hydrogen chloride, hypochlorites, chlorides, and bleaching powder, which are used in disinfection and chemical production.

Interhalogen compounds are formed by the combination of two different halogen elements, such as ClF, BrF₃, and IF₅. They are generally covalent and reactive, and their structures depend on the relative sizes and bonding characteristics of the halogen atoms.

topics.topic: Uses of non-metals and their compounds
topics.brief: Non-metals and their compounds are essential in industry, agriculture, medicine, and everyday life. Examples include oxygen for respiration and medical use, nitrogen compounds for fertilisers, chlorine for water disinfection, and sulphuric acid for industrial manufacturing.

Metals generally have metallic lustre, good electrical and thermal conductivity, and are malleable and ductile. Most are solids at room temperature and tend to lose electrons to form positive ions, although some metals have unusual physical properties.

Metals occur in Earth's crust in either native form or combined form. Less reactive metals, such as gold, may occur naturally as free elements, while many others occur in minerals and ores as oxides, sulphides, carbonates, or other compounds.

Minerals are naturally occurring substances containing elements or compounds in the Earth's crust. An ore is a mineral or mineral deposit from which a metal can be extracted conveniently and economically using available methods.

Concentration of ore, also called ore dressing or beneficiation, removes unwanted earthy materials known as gangue. The method selected depends on differences in physical or chemical properties between the valuable mineral and the impurities.
Crushing and grinding reduce large pieces of ore to smaller particles. This increases the surface area and helps separate valuable minerals from gangue during subsequent concentration processes.

Gravity separation concentrates ores by exploiting differences in density between the valuable mineral and gangue. A stream of water or another suitable medium carries away lighter particles while denser mineral particles are retained.

Magnetic separation uses differences in magnetic properties to separate valuable minerals from unwanted materials. Magnetic particles are attracted by a magnetic field, allowing them to be collected separately from non-magnetic particles.

Froth flotation is commonly used to concentrate sulphide ores. Finely ground ore is mixed with water and suitable reagents, allowing mineral particles to attach to air bubbles and rise with the froth while much of the gangue remains in the liquid.

Leaching separates a desired substance by selectively dissolving it in a suitable chemical solution. The dissolved metal compound can then be recovered from the solution through processes such as precipitation or electrolysis.

Calcination involves heating an ore strongly in limited or no air to cause thermal decomposition and remove volatile substances. It is commonly used for carbonate and hydrated ores, often converting them into metal oxides.

Roasting involves heating an ore strongly in excess air or oxygen. It is commonly used for sulphide ores to convert them into oxides and release sulphur dioxide, although the exact reactions depend on the ore.

Reduction of metal oxides removes oxygen from the oxide to produce the metal. Depending on the metal's reactivity, reduction may use carbon, carbon monoxide, hydrogen, a more reactive metal, or an electrolytic process.

Smelting is a high-temperature extraction process in which an ore is heated with suitable reducing agents and fluxes to obtain a molten metal or metal-containing product. Flux reacts with gangue to form slag, which can be separated from the metal.

Electrolytic extraction uses electrical energy to reduce metal ions and obtain metals from molten compounds or suitable solutions. It is especially important for highly reactive metals, such as aluminium, that cannot be extracted easily by ordinary carbon reduction.

Refining removes impurities from crude metals to improve their purity and properties. Methods include electrolytic refining, distillation, liquation, and zone refining, with the appropriate method depending on the metal and the nature of its impurities.

The reactivity series arranges metals in order of their tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions. It helps predict displacement reactions, reactions with water and acids, and the methods suitable for extracting metals from their ores.

Iron is commonly extracted from iron ores, such as haematite, in a blast furnace. Coke produces heat and carbon monoxide, which helps reduce iron oxides, while limestone acts as a flux that combines with impurities to form slag.

Aluminium is extracted mainly from purified alumina obtained from bauxite. The alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite and electrolysed, allowing aluminium to form at the cathode; the process requires substantial electrical energy.

Copper can be extracted from sulphide ores through processes that may include concentration, roasting, smelting, and converting. Copper obtained from smelting can be further purified by electrolytic refining to produce high-purity metal.

Zinc is commonly extracted from zinc blende (sphalerite) or other zinc ores. Zinc sulphide ore is usually roasted to form zinc oxide, which is then reduced using carbon or carbon monoxide before the zinc is collected and refined.

Alloys are materials made by combining a metal with one or more other elements. Alloying can improve properties such as strength, hardness, corrosion resistance, and durability; common examples include steel, brass, and bronze.

Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal through chemical or electrochemical reactions with its environment. Rusting of iron is a familiar example and generally requires moisture and oxygen, while other metals can form different corrosion products.

Corrosion can be reduced by painting, oiling, greasing, protective coatings, galvanising, alloying, or electrochemical methods such as cathodic protection. The best method depends on the metal, the environment, and the intended use.

Metals and alloys are widely used in construction, transport, electrical systems, machinery, packaging, and medical equipment. Iron and steel are important structural materials, copper is used in electrical wiring, and aluminium is valued for its low density and corrosion resistance.

topics.topic: Role of inorganic elements in living organisms
topics.brief: Inorganic elements are essential for many biological processes, including nerve signalling, muscle contraction, oxygen transport, enzyme function, and maintaining fluid balance. Their effects depend on the element, its chemical form, and its concentration in the body.

Essential elements are required for normal growth, development, and physiological function. Trace elements are needed in very small quantities; examples include iron, zinc, copper, iodine, and selenium, although excessive amounts of some essential elements can be harmful.

topics.topic: Biological importance of sodium and potassium
topics.brief: Sodium and potassium are electrolytes that help maintain fluid balance, osmotic pressure, and electrical activity in cells. Their concentration gradients across cell membranes are important for nerve impulses, muscle contraction, and the transport of substances.

topics.topic: Biological importance of calcium and magnesium
topics.brief: Calcium is important for bones and teeth, muscle contraction, blood clotting, and cell signalling. Magnesium contributes to bone structure, supports many enzymes, and is central to the chlorophyll molecule in plants.

topics.topic: Role of iron in biological systems
topics.brief: Iron is an essential trace element involved in oxygen transport, cellular respiration, and electron-transfer reactions. It forms part of haemoglobin, myoglobin, and several enzymes that help cells use energy and carry out metabolic processes.

Haemoglobin is an iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen reversibly in the lungs and releases it in tissues. Its ability to transport oxygen depends on the chemical environment, including oxygen concentration, pH, and carbon dioxide levels.

topics.topic: Role of cobalt in vitamin B12
topics.brief: Cobalt is the central metal ion in vitamin B₁₂, also known as cobalamin. This vitamin supports red blood cell formation, DNA synthesis, and normal nervous system function, and it must be obtained through suitable dietary sources or supplementation when needed.

Zinc is an essential trace element that supports the structure or catalytic activity of many enzymes. Zinc-dependent enzymes participate in processes such as digestion, DNA synthesis, cell repair, and metabolism.

topics.topic: Role of iodine in thyroid hormones
topics.brief: Iodine is required for the production of thyroid hormones, mainly thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃). These hormones help regulate metabolism, growth, development, and body temperature; both iodine deficiency and excessive intake can disrupt thyroid function.

Metal ions such as Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, and Cu²⁺ act as cofactors for many enzymes. They may help stabilise structures, bind substrates, transfer electrons, or support chemical reactions, and their availability can influence enzyme activity.

Electrolytes are substances that form ions when dissolved in body fluids and allow electrical charge to move. Sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and bicarbonate help regulate fluid balance, nerve and muscle function, and acid-base balance.

Calcium and phosphate are major mineral components of bones and teeth, primarily in the form of hydroxyapatite. These minerals provide hardness and structural support, while other nutrients and biological processes help maintain healthy bone and tooth tissues.

Some metals and metalloids, including lead, mercury, and cadmium, can be toxic when exposure is sufficient. They may damage the nervous system, kidneys, blood-forming tissues, or other organs, with effects depending on the substance, dose, route, and duration of exposure.

Coordination compounds contain a central metal ion bonded to surrounding ligands. They are important in biology; examples include haemoglobin, which contains an iron coordination centre, and vitamin B₁₂, which contains cobalt. Such structures enable specialised functions such as oxygen transport and enzyme activity.

Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies carbon compounds, particularly hydrocarbons and their derivatives. It covers their structures, properties, preparation, reactions, and applications in living systems and industry.

Carbon forms a remarkably large number of compounds because of its tetravalency, ability to form strong covalent bonds, and capacity to bond with itself and many other elements. These properties allow carbon to form chains, rings, and complex molecular structures.

Tetravalency is the ability of carbon to form four covalent bonds with other atoms. Catenation is the ability of an element to form bonds with atoms of the same element, allowing carbon to create long chains, branched structures, and rings.

Organic compounds can be classified according to their carbon skeleton, functional groups, and bonding patterns. Major categories include acyclic and cyclic compounds, saturated and unsaturated compounds, and compounds containing specific functional groups.

Open-chain compounds have carbon atoms arranged in straight or branched chains without forming a ring. Cyclic compounds contain one or more rings of atoms and may be saturated, unsaturated, carbocyclic, or heterocyclic.
Homocyclic compounds contain rings made entirely of carbon atoms. Heterocyclic compounds contain at least one non-carbon atom, such as nitrogen, oxygen, or sulphur, within the ring structure.

Saturated compounds contain only carbon-carbon single bonds in their carbon skeletons, as in alkanes. Unsaturated compounds contain one or more carbon-carbon double or triple bonds, as in alkenes and alkynes.

A functional group is an atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic chemical reactions of an organic compound. Examples include hydroxyl (-OH), aldehyde (-CHO), carboxyl (-COOH), amino (-NH₂), and carbonyl (>C=O) groups.

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members usually differ by a -CH₂- unit. Members have similar chemical properties and show gradual changes in physical properties.

IUPAC nomenclature is the systematic method for naming chemical compounds according to internationally agreed rules. Organic names are generally constructed by identifying the parent chain or ring, numbering it appropriately, and specifying substituents, functional groups, and bond positions.

Common nomenclature uses traditional or historically established names for organic compounds rather than fully systematic IUPAC names. Examples include acetone for propanone and acetic acid for ethanoic acid.

A structural formula shows how atoms are connected within a molecule. It provides more information than a molecular formula because it represents the arrangement of bonds and helps distinguish compounds with the same molecular formula.

Condensed structural formulae represent atom groupings in a compact form, such as CH₃CH₂OH. Skeletal formulae use lines to represent carbon-carbon bonds, with carbon atoms and many hydrogen atoms attached to carbon omitted for simplicity.
Structural isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms. Common types include chain, position, functional group, and metameric isomerism.

Chain isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of the carbon skeleton. For example, butane and 2-methylpropane are chain isomers with the formula C₄H₁₀.

Position isomerism occurs when compounds have the same carbon skeleton and functional group but differ in the position of a substituent, functional group, or multiple bond. For example, propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are position isomers.

Functional group isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different functional groups. For example, ethanol and methoxymethane both have the formula C₂H₆O but belong to different functional classes.

Metamerism is a type of structural isomerism found in certain compounds containing a polyvalent functional group or atom between carbon groups. The isomers differ in the distribution of carbon atoms on either side of that group, as in some ethers and secondary amines.

Tautomerism is a dynamic equilibrium between structural forms that differ mainly in the position of a proton and a double bond. Keto-enol tautomerism is a common example, involving interconversion between a carbonyl-containing form and an enol form.

Geometrical isomerism is a type of stereoisomerism caused by restricted rotation, commonly around a carbon-carbon double bond or within a ring. Cis-trans or E-Z isomers differ in the spatial arrangement of groups despite having the same connectivity.

Optical isomerism occurs when molecules exist as non-superimposable mirror images called enantiomers. It commonly arises from chirality, such as a carbon atom bonded to four different groups, and enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

The inductive effect is the permanent displacement of electron density along sigma bonds due to differences in electronegativity. Electron-withdrawing groups show a negative inductive effect (-I), while electron-releasing groups show a positive inductive effect (+I).

The resonance effect occurs when electrons are delocalised across a conjugated system and a molecule is represented by multiple contributing structures. Delocalisation can increase stability and influence acidity, basicity, and the course of chemical reactions.

The electromeric effect is a temporary complete transfer of pi-electrons in a multiple bond under the influence of an attacking reagent. It disappears when the reagent is removed and is commonly discussed in reactions involving double or triple bonds.

Hyperconjugation is the delocalisation of electrons from a sigma bond, commonly a C-H or C-C bond, into an adjacent pi system or vacant p orbital. It helps explain the stability of certain carbocations, alkenes, and substituted organic structures.

Homolytic bond fission occurs when a covalent bond breaks evenly, with each bonded atom receiving one electron. This process produces free radicals and is often promoted by heat, ultraviolet light, or radical initiators.
Heterolytic bond fission occurs when a covalent bond breaks unevenly and both bonding electrons go to one atom. It produces oppositely charged ions, such as a carbocation and a leaving-group anion.

Free radicals are atoms or groups of atoms containing an unpaired electron. They are often highly reactive and can participate in chain reactions, including halogenation of alkanes and some polymerisation processes.

Carbocations are positively charged carbon-containing species in which a carbon atom has an electron deficiency. Their stability is influenced by alkyl groups, resonance, and hyperconjugation; in many simple cases, tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary and primary ones.

Carbanions are negatively charged carbon-containing species in which carbon has a lone pair of electrons. Their stability depends on factors such as resonance, electronegativity, hybridisation, and electron-withdrawing groups.

Electrophiles are electron-deficient species that accept an electron pair to form a bond. Nucleophiles are electron-rich species that donate an electron pair to form a bond; examples include H⁺ as an electrophile and OH⁻ as a nucleophile.
Organic reactions are classified according to the changes occurring in molecules. Major types include substitution, addition, elimination, rearrangement, oxidation, and reduction reactions.

A substitution reaction occurs when an atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group. Examples include free-radical halogenation of alkanes and electrophilic substitution reactions of aromatic compounds.

An addition reaction occurs when atoms or groups add across a multiple bond, often converting an unsaturated compound into a more saturated product. Alkenes, for example, undergo addition with hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides, and water under suitable conditions.

An elimination reaction removes atoms or groups from a molecule, often creating a carbon-carbon double or triple bond. For example, dehydration of an alcohol can produce an alkene under suitable conditions.

Rearrangement reactions involve the reorganisation of atoms or groups within a molecule to form a structural isomer or a product with a different carbon framework. They commonly proceed through intermediates and are influenced by the stability of the resulting structure.

Purification removes unwanted impurities from an organic compound to obtain a substance of suitable purity. Common methods include crystallisation, distillation, sublimation, and chromatography, selected according to differences in physical or chemical properties.

Crystallisation purifies a solid by dissolving it in a suitable hot solvent and allowing crystals to form as the solution cools or the solvent evaporates. Impurities may remain in the solution or be removed by filtration.

Distillation separates or purifies liquids using differences in volatility and boiling points. Simple distillation is useful when boiling points differ substantially, while fractional distillation is commonly used for liquids with closer boiling points.

Sublimation is the direct conversion of a solid into vapour without passing through the liquid state. It can be used to purify sublimable substances, such as iodine or naphthalene, from non-sublimable impurities.

Chromatography separates mixture components according to their different interactions with a stationary phase and a mobile phase. Common forms include paper, thin-layer, column, and gas chromatography, which are used for separation, identification, and purity analysis.

Qualitative analysis identifies elements and functional groups present in an organic compound. Elemental tests may detect nitrogen, sulphur, and halogens, while characteristic chemical tests help identify groups such as alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids.

Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. They are classified into aliphatic hydrocarbons, including alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes, and aromatic hydrocarbons, which contain characteristic conjugated ring systems such as benzene.

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only carbon-carbon single bonds. Acyclic alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and are relatively unreactive under ordinary conditions compared with unsaturated hydrocarbons.

Alkanes are named using IUPAC rules by selecting the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent, numbering it to give substituents the lowest possible locants, and naming branches as alkyl groups. The suffix '-ane' identifies the saturated parent hydrocarbon.

Alkanes can be prepared by methods such as hydrogenation of alkenes or alkynes, reduction of suitable alkyl halides, decarboxylation of carboxylate salts, and the Wurtz reaction. The method chosen depends on the required alkane and the starting materials.

Alkanes are non-polar substances that are generally insoluble in water but soluble in many non-polar organic solvents. Their boiling points usually increase with molecular size and decrease with branching among structural isomers; smaller alkanes are gases, while larger ones are liquids or solids at room temperature.

Alkanes are relatively unreactive because their carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen bonds are strong and largely non-polar. Important reactions include combustion, free-radical substitution with halogens, and thermal or catalytic cracking under appropriate conditions.

Alkanes burn in sufficient oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy. In limited oxygen, incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide or carbon, making it less efficient and potentially hazardous.

Free-radical substitution is a chain reaction in which an atom, commonly hydrogen in an alkane, is replaced by another atom such as chlorine or bromine. The mechanism includes initiation, propagation, and termination steps and is often started by ultraviolet light or heat.

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond. Acyclic alkenes with one double bond generally have the formula CₙH₂ₙ and commonly undergo addition reactions across the double bond.

Alkenes are named by selecting the longest chain containing the double bond and numbering it so the double bond receives the lowest possible locant. The parent name uses the suffix '-ene', and substituents and stereochemistry are included when needed.

Alkenes can be prepared by elimination reactions, including dehydration of alcohols and dehydrohalogenation of suitable alkyl halides. The reaction conditions and substrate structure influence the product and the position of the double bond.

Alkenes are generally non-polar or weakly polar, insoluble in water, and soluble in many organic solvents. Their physical properties depend on molecular size and structure, and their boiling points usually increase as molecular mass increases.

Alkenes commonly undergo addition reactions because the pi bond in the carbon-carbon double bond is relatively accessible to reacting species. Typical reactions include hydrogenation, halogenation, hydrohalogenation, and hydration, producing more saturated compounds.

Markovnikov's rule predicts the major product in many additions of hydrogen halides to unsymmetrical alkenes: hydrogen generally attaches to the double-bond carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms, while the halide attaches to the other carbon. The rule applies to typical ionic addition conditions.

The peroxide effect refers to anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr to certain unsymmetrical alkenes through a free-radical mechanism in the presence of peroxides. This effect is characteristic of HBr and is not normally observed in the same way with HCl or HI.

Alkenes undergo oxidation reactions that depend on the oxidising agent and conditions. Mild oxidation can produce vicinal diols, while stronger oxidative cleavage can break the carbon-carbon double bond to form carbonyl compounds or carboxylic acids.

Polymerisation joins many alkene molecules, called monomers, to form long-chain polymers through their double bonds. Examples include ethene forming polyethene and propene forming polypropene, both of which are widely used plastics.

Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon triple bond. Acyclic alkynes with one triple bond generally have the formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ and undergo addition reactions at the triple bond.

Alkynes are named by choosing the longest carbon chain containing the triple bond and numbering it to give the triple bond the lowest possible locant. The suffix '-yne' identifies the triple bond, and substituents are named and numbered using standard IUPAC rules.

Alkynes can be prepared by double dehydrohalogenation of suitable dihalogenated compounds. Ethyne can also be prepared by reacting calcium carbide with water, producing ethyne gas and calcium hydroxide.
