Alkynes undergo addition reactions with hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides, and water under suitable conditions. They can also be oxidised, and terminal alkynes may form acetylide salts because their terminal hydrogen is relatively acidic.

Terminal alkynes contain a hydrogen attached to an sp-hybridised carbon, making them more acidic than alkenes and alkanes. Strong bases can remove this hydrogen to form acetylide ions, which are useful in carbon-carbon bond-forming reactions.

Hydrogenation adds hydrogen across carbon-carbon double or triple bonds, usually with a metal catalyst such as nickel, palladium, or platinum. Alkenes can be converted into alkanes, while alkynes may be reduced to alkenes or alkanes depending on the conditions and catalyst.

Unsaturation can be detected using reagents such as bromine solution or dilute alkaline potassium permanganate under appropriate conditions. Alkenes and alkynes may decolourise these reagents through addition or oxidation reactions, although test results must be interpreted with care because other substances can also react.

Hydrocarbons are important fuels and raw materials for the chemical industry. They are used in petrol, diesel, natural gas, lubricants, solvents, plastics, synthetic fibres, and the manufacture of many other organic chemicals.

Hydrocarbon combustion releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, and incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide and soot. Fuel combustion can also contribute to nitrogen oxide emissions and air pollution, with impacts on climate, health, and ecosystems.

Aromaticity is a special stabilisation associated with cyclic, planar, conjugated systems containing delocalised pi electrons. In the usual introductory model, a planar monocyclic system is aromatic when it has 4n+2 pi electrons, where n is a non-negative integer.

Benzene (C₆H₆) is a planar six-carbon ring in which each carbon is bonded to one hydrogen. Its six pi electrons are delocalised around the ring, making all carbon-carbon bonds equivalent in length rather than alternating between distinct single and double bonds.

Resonance describes benzene using multiple contributing structures with different arrangements of formal double bonds. The actual molecule is a resonance hybrid with delocalised pi electrons, equivalent carbon-carbon bonds, and greater stability than a simple localised-bond model predicts.

Kekule structures represent benzene as a six-membered carbon ring with alternating single and double bonds. Two equivalent Kekule forms can be drawn, but neither alone fully describes the actual delocalised electron structure of benzene.

Benzene has unusual stability due to aromatic delocalisation of its six pi electrons. This stabilisation helps explain why benzene typically undergoes substitution reactions rather than the addition reactions commonly shown by ordinary alkenes.

Aromatic compounds are named by treating benzene as the parent in many simple cases and identifying attached substituents with appropriate positions. Disubstituted benzenes may be described using ortho (1,2-), meta (1,3-), and para (1,4-) terminology, while systematic IUPAC names use numerical locants.

Benzene can be prepared by several chemical methods, including decarboxylation of suitable aromatic carboxylate salts, trimerisation of ethyne under appropriate conditions, and dehydrogenation of cyclohexane. Industrial production commonly involves processing petroleum-derived feedstocks.

Benzene is a colourless, volatile liquid with a characteristic odour and limited solubility in water. It dissolves in many organic solvents and is flammable; benzene is also a known human carcinogen, so exposure must be strictly controlled.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution is a reaction in which an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on an aromatic ring while aromaticity is restored. Common examples include nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, and Friedel-Crafts reactions.

Nitration introduces a nitro group (-NO₂) into the benzene ring. Benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulphuric acid under controlled conditions, generating the electrophile that forms nitrobenzene.

Sulphonation introduces a sulphonic acid group (-SO₃H) into the benzene ring. It is typically carried out using fuming sulphuric acid or sulphur trioxide in sulphuric acid, and the reaction can be reversible under suitable conditions.

Halogenation replaces a hydrogen atom on benzene with a halogen such as chlorine or bromine. It commonly requires a Lewis acid catalyst, such as FeCl₃ or FeBr₃, to generate a sufficiently reactive electrophile.

Friedel-Crafts alkylation introduces an alkyl group into an aromatic ring using an alkylating reagent and a Lewis acid catalyst, commonly AlCl₃. The reaction can suffer from rearrangements and multiple alkylation, depending on the substrate and conditions.

Friedel-Crafts acylation introduces an acyl group (-COR) into an aromatic ring, commonly using an acyl chloride or acid anhydride with a Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl₃. It produces an aromatic ketone and generally avoids the carbocation rearrangements associated with many alkylation reactions.

Groups already attached to a benzene ring influence both the rate and position of further electrophilic substitution. Many electron-donating groups direct incoming substituents to ortho and para positions, while many electron-withdrawing groups direct them to the meta position; halogens are an important exception because they are deactivating but ortho-para directing.

Alkylbenzenes can undergo reactions at the side chain as well as at the aromatic ring. Under suitable radical conditions, benzylic hydrogen atoms can be substituted by halogens, while strong oxidation can convert an alkyl side chain with a benzylic hydrogen into a carboxyl group.

topics.topic: Environmental and health effects of aromatic hydrocarbons
topics.brief: Some aromatic hydrocarbons contribute to air pollution and may harm human health. Benzene is carcinogenic, while other aromatic compounds can affect the nervous system or contribute to smog; risks depend on the compound, concentration, exposure route, and duration.

Chemistry plays an important role in household products such as soaps, detergents, cleaners, cosmetics, and disinfectants. Their chemical ingredients determine properties such as cleaning ability, stability, fragrance, and safety.

Soaps are generally sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids, while detergents are cleansing agents that may contain synthetic surfactants. Both help remove dirt and grease by reducing surface tension and allowing oily substances to mix with water.

Soap molecules have a hydrophilic head that interacts with water and a hydrophobic tail that interacts with grease. They form micelles around oily dirt, allowing it to become suspended in water and be removed during rinsing.

Hard water contains calcium and magnesium ions that react with soap to form insoluble scum, reducing its cleaning efficiency. Many synthetic detergents work better in hard water because they do not readily form insoluble precipitates with these ions.

Food additives are substances added to food to improve or maintain its flavour, colour, texture, stability, or shelf life. Examples include preservatives, antioxidants, emulsifiers, stabilisers, flavour enhancers, and approved colouring agents.

Preservatives help prevent or slow food spoilage caused by microorganisms or chemical reactions. Examples include sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate, while salt, sugar, and vinegar can also help preserve food under suitable conditions.

Artificial and other high-intensity sweeteners provide a sweet taste with little or no energy at the quantities normally used. Examples include aspartame, saccharin, and sucralose; their safety and permitted uses depend on regulatory limits and individual circumstances.

Flavouring agents provide or enhance the taste and aroma of food, while colouring agents improve or restore its appearance. These substances may be natural or synthetic, and only suitable food-grade additives should be used within permitted limits.

Medicines contain active substances used to prevent, diagnose, manage, or treat diseases. Pharmaceutical chemistry studies their structures, properties, preparation, stability, and interactions with biological systems.

Antiseptics are substances used on living tissues to reduce or inhibit microorganisms, whereas disinfectants are generally used on non-living surfaces. Their effectiveness depends on factors such as concentration, contact time, and the type of microorganism.

Fertilisers supply essential plant nutrients that support growth and crop production. Major nutrients include nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium; excessive or poorly managed fertiliser use can cause nutrient runoff, water pollution, and soil-related problems.

Pesticides are substances used to control pests, including insects, weeds, fungi, and rodents. Insecticides specifically target insects; improper use can harm non-target organisms, contaminate the environment, and create risks to human health.

Polymers are large molecules made of repeating structural units called monomers. Everyday examples include polyethylene packaging, PVC pipes, nylon fibres, polyester fabrics, rubber products, and biological polymers such as proteins and cellulose.

Chemical safety involves handling, storing, transporting, and disposing of chemicals in ways that minimise harm. Product labels provide information about hazards, precautions, ingredients, first aid, and storage; hazard pictograms and safety data sheets help users assess risks.

Consumer chemicals can enter air, water, and soil during use or disposal. Some may persist in the environment, harm aquatic organisms, or contribute to pollution, so safer product choices, correct disposal, and reduced unnecessary chemical use are important.

Environmental chemistry studies chemical processes occurring in the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, and living systems. It examines the sources, reactions, movement, and effects of natural and human-made substances in the environment.

Air pollution occurs when gases, particles, or biological materials enter the atmosphere at concentrations that harm people, other organisms, or the environment. Major sources include vehicle exhaust, industries, power generation, waste burning, and household fuel combustion.

Water pollution occurs when harmful substances or microorganisms contaminate rivers, lakes, groundwater, or other water bodies. Common sources include untreated sewage, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff, plastics, and oil spills.

Soil pollution is the accumulation of harmful chemicals or wastes in soil at levels that can affect organisms, food production, or ecosystems. Sources include pesticides, industrial waste, heavy metals, petroleum spills, and improper disposal of household waste.

Major air pollutants include particulate matter, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, ground-level ozone, and volatile organic compounds. Their sources and effects vary, and some pollutants also contribute to smog, acid rain, or the formation of secondary pollutants.

Particulate matter consists of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air. PM₁₀ includes particles with aerodynamic diameters of 10 micrometres or less, while PM₂.₅ includes finer particles that can penetrate deeply into the lungs and contribute to cardiovascular and respiratory illness.

Acid rain refers to precipitation that is more acidic than normal, mainly because sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form sulphuric and nitric acids in the atmosphere. It can acidify lakes and soils, damage vegetation, and accelerate the deterioration of buildings and monuments.

Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ground-level ozone and other oxidants. It is common in polluted urban areas and can irritate the eyes and respiratory system while damaging crops and materials.

The greenhouse effect is the warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit some outgoing infrared radiation. The natural greenhouse effect makes Earth habitable, while increased greenhouse gas concentrations enhance warming.

Global warming is the long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily driven by human emissions of greenhouse gases from fossil fuels, deforestation, and other activities. Its impacts include rising sea levels, heatwaves, changing rainfall patterns, and increased risks to ecosystems and human communities.

Ozone depletion is the reduction of ozone concentration in the stratosphere, mainly caused by human-made substances that release chlorine or bromine radicals. A thinner ozone layer allows more harmful ultraviolet radiation to reach Earth's surface, increasing risks to human health and ecosystems.

Water quality describes the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics that determine whether water is suitable for drinking, agriculture, industry, or aquatic life. Important indicators include pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, microbial contamination, and concentrations of dissolved substances.

Water purification removes suspended particles, dissolved contaminants, and harmful microorganisms to make water suitable for a particular use. Common processes include sedimentation, filtration, coagulation, disinfection, and, where necessary, specialised treatments such as activated carbon or membrane filtration.

Chemical oxygen demand (COD) measures the oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise substances in a water sample under specified test conditions. It is commonly used to assess the level of oxidisable pollution in wastewater and is usually expressed in milligrams of oxygen per litre.

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) measures the oxygen consumed by microorganisms while decomposing biodegradable organic matter in water under defined conditions. The five-day BOD test, commonly reported as BOD₅, is widely used to assess organic pollution; high BOD can reduce dissolved oxygen available to aquatic organisms.

Waste management includes the collection, segregation, treatment, recycling, recovery, and safe disposal of waste. The waste hierarchy prioritises prevention and reduction, followed by reuse and recycling, with treatment and disposal used for materials that cannot be managed more sustainably.

Industrial chemical pollution occurs when industrial activities release harmful chemicals into air, water, or soil. Potential pollutants include heavy metals, solvents, acids, alkalis, and persistent organic compounds; monitoring, treatment, process controls, and safe waste management help reduce their impacts.

Sustainable chemistry aims to design chemical products and processes that reduce hazardous substances, energy use, waste, and environmental damage. Green chemistry principles encourage renewable feedstocks, safer solvents, efficient catalysts, and reactions that maximise the use of starting materials.

Pollution prevention reduces or eliminates pollutants at their source rather than relying only on treatment after they are produced. Strategies include cleaner production, energy efficiency, safer chemical substitution, waste minimisation, recycling, and improved environmental management.

Volumetric analysis is a quantitative analytical method used to determine the concentration or amount of a substance by measuring the volume of a reacting solution. Titration is one of its most common techniques.
A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent. Concentration expresses the amount of solute present in a specified amount of solution or solvent.
A solute is the substance dissolved in a solution, while the solvent is the substance that dissolves it. In an aqueous solution, water acts as the solvent.
Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per litre of solution. It is expressed in mol/L and is calculated by dividing the moles of solute by the solution volume in litres.
Molality is the number of moles of solute dissolved per kilogram of solvent. Unlike molarity, it is independent of solution volume changes caused by temperature.
Normality expresses the number of gram-equivalents of solute per litre of solution. Its value depends on the reaction being considered because the equivalent factor may differ between reactions.
Mole fraction is the ratio of the moles of one component to the total moles of all components in a mixture. The mole fractions of all components add up to one.
Mass percentage gives the mass of a component divided by the total mass of the solution, multiplied by 100. It is useful for expressing the composition of solutions and mixtures.
Volume percentage is the volume of a component divided by the total volume of the solution, multiplied by 100. It is commonly used to describe mixtures of liquids.

Parts per million (ppm) expresses the amount of a substance relative to one million parts of a mixture. For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 ppm is approximately equivalent to 1 mg/L when the solution density is close to that of water.

A standard solution has a known concentration and is prepared by accurately measuring a suitable amount of solute and dissolving it to a specified final volume. Accurate weighing, transfer, and use of volumetric glassware are essential.

A primary standard is a highly pure, stable substance with a known composition that can be weighed directly to prepare a solution of accurately known concentration. It should ideally be non-hygroscopic and have a relatively high molar mass.

A secondary standard is a solution whose exact concentration must be determined by standardisation against a primary standard or another reliable reference. Such solutions may change concentration during storage.

Standardisation determines the exact concentration of a solution by reacting it with a standard substance or solution of known concentration. It is important when a solution cannot be prepared accurately by direct weighing alone.

Titration is a quantitative technique in which a solution of known concentration is added gradually to a measured amount of another solution until the reaction reaches the required endpoint. The volume used helps determine the unknown concentration.

Acid-base indicators are substances whose colours change over a particular pH range. Examples include phenolphthalein and methyl orange, which help indicate the approximate endpoint of acid-base titrations.

The equivalence point is the point in a titration at which the reacting substances have been mixed in the stoichiometric proportions specified by the balanced chemical equation. It is a theoretical reaction point.

The endpoint is the experimentally observed point at which an indicator changes colour or an instrument signals completion. A suitable indicator is chosen so that its endpoint lies close to the equivalence point.

Acid-base titration determines the concentration of an acid or base through a neutralisation reaction with a standard solution. The calculation uses the balanced equation and the measured volumes and concentrations.

Redox titration determines concentration through an oxidation-reduction reaction involving electron transfer. Common titrants include potassium permanganate and iodine solutions, depending on the substance being analysed.

Oxidation-reduction indicators change colour between oxidised and reduced forms at characteristic electrode potentials. They can help identify the endpoint of redox titrations when the titrant itself does not provide a clear colour change.

Titration calculations use measured volumes, known concentrations, and the mole ratios from a balanced equation to determine an unknown quantity. The calculation must account for the stoichiometric coefficients of the reacting substances.

Experimental errors may arise from inaccurate readings, air bubbles in burettes, incorrect indicator choice, contaminated glassware, or overshooting the endpoint. Repeating measurements and using proper laboratory technique improve reliability.

Electrolytes produce mobile ions in molten form or aqueous solution and can conduct electricity. Non-electrolytes do not produce sufficient mobile ions under the same conditions to conduct electricity effectively.

Strong electrolytes ionise or dissociate almost completely in solution, while weak electrolytes ionise only partially. The distinction concerns the extent of ionisation, not simply the concentration of the solution.

Ionisation is the formation of ions when a substance interacts with a solvent, while dissociation is the separation of pre-existing ions in an ionic compound. Weak electrolytes establish an equilibrium between ionised and unionised forms.

topics.topic: Arrhenius concept of acids and bases
topics.brief: According to the Arrhenius concept, an acid increases the concentration of H⁺ or H₃O⁺ ions in aqueous solution, while a base increases the concentration of OH⁻ ions. This model primarily applies to aqueous solutions.
The Brønsted-Lowry concept defines an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor. It explains acid-base reactions in aqueous and non-aqueous systems through proton transfer.

topics.topic: Lewis concept of acids and bases
topics.brief: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair, while a Lewis base donates an electron pair to form a coordinate covalent bond. This concept includes reactions that do not involve proton transfer.
A conjugate acid-base pair consists of two species that differ by one proton. When an acid donates a proton, it forms its conjugate base; when a base accepts a proton, it forms its conjugate acid.
The acid ionisation constant, Ka, measures the extent to which an acid ionises in solution at equilibrium. A larger Ka generally indicates a stronger acid under comparable conditions.
The base ionisation constant, Kb, measures the extent to which a base reacts with water to produce its conjugate acid and hydroxide ions. A larger Kb generally indicates a stronger base.
pH expresses the acidity of a solution and is defined using hydrogen-ion activity, while pOH describes hydroxide-ion activity. In dilute aqueous solutions near 25°C, pH + pOH is approximately 14.

Water undergoes slight self-ionisation, in which one water molecule transfers a proton to another. This process produces hydronium and hydroxide ions and establishes an equilibrium even in pure water.

The ionic product of water, Kw, is the product of the equilibrium concentrations or activities of hydronium and hydroxide ions. At 25°C, its concentration-based value in dilute water is approximately 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.

The common ion effect is the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte or the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt when another substance supplies an ion already present in the equilibrium.
A buffer solution resists large changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It commonly contains a weak acid and its conjugate base or a weak base and its conjugate acid.
An acidic buffer typically contains a weak acid and its salt with a strong base, while a basic buffer contains a weak base and its salt with a strong acid. Each maintains pH within a useful range.

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relates buffer pH to the pKa of a weak acid and the ratio of conjugate-base concentration to acid concentration. It is useful for estimating buffer pH when the assumptions behind the equation are satisfied.

Salt hydrolysis occurs when ions from a dissolved salt react with water and affect the solution's pH. The resulting solution may be acidic, basic, or approximately neutral depending on the strengths of the parent acid and base.

Solubility equilibrium is established when a dissolved substance and its undissolved solid coexist at a constant temperature with no net change in dissolution or precipitation. The equilibrium depends on temperature and the composition of the solution.

The solubility product constant, Ksp, is the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a sparingly soluble ionic solid. It is written using the equilibrium activities or concentrations of the dissolved ions, each raised to its stoichiometric power.

topics.topic: Relationship between solubility and solubility product
topics.brief: The relationship between molar solubility and Ksp is obtained by expressing the equilibrium ion concentrations in terms of the amount of solid dissolved. The resulting expression depends on the salt's formula and the stoichiometry of its dissolution.

A precipitation reaction occurs when dissolved ions combine to form a sparingly soluble solid. Comparing the ion product with Ksp helps predict whether precipitation is thermodynamically favoured under the stated conditions.

Ionic equilibrium helps explain buffer action, acid-base behaviour, salt hydrolysis, selective precipitation, and the solubility of ionic compounds. It is used in analytical chemistry, water treatment, biological systems, and industrial processes.
The rate of a chemical reaction describes how quickly reactant concentrations decrease or product concentrations increase with time. It is commonly expressed as a concentration change per unit time.

Average reaction rate is calculated from the concentration change of a reactant or product over a specified time interval. Stoichiometric coefficients are used when expressing a single overall reaction rate.
Instantaneous reaction rate is the rate at a particular moment in time. On a concentration-time graph, it corresponds to the slope of the tangent to the curve at that moment.

Reaction rates can be affected by concentration, pressure for gases, temperature, surface area, catalysts, and the nature of the reactants. These factors influence collision frequency, activation barriers, or the reaction pathway.

Changing reactant concentration can change reaction rate by altering the frequency of effective molecular encounters. The precise relationship is determined experimentally and is expressed through the rate law.

A rate law expresses reaction rate as a mathematical relationship involving reactant concentrations raised to experimentally determined powers. These powers generally cannot be inferred from the balanced chemical equation alone.

The rate constant is the proportionality constant in a rate law at a specified temperature. Its units depend on the overall reaction order, and its value may change with temperature or the presence of a catalyst.
The order of a reaction is the sum of the powers of concentration terms in its experimentally determined rate law. Individual orders may be zero, integer, or fractional values.

Molecularity is the number of reacting particles involved in a single elementary reaction step. It is always a positive integer for an elementary step and should not be confused with the experimentally determined overall reaction order.

In a zero-order reaction, the rate is independent of the concentration of the specified reactant over the applicable range. Its integrated rate equation predicts a linear decrease in reactant concentration with time.

A first-order reaction has a rate directly proportional to the concentration of one reactant. Its integrated rate equation gives a linear relationship between the natural logarithm of concentration and time.

A second-order reaction has a rate law whose concentration exponents add to two. For a simple reaction with rate proportional to the square of one reactant concentration, the reciprocal concentration changes linearly with time.

Integrated rate equations relate reactant concentration to time for reactions with specified rate laws. They allow reaction order, rate constants, and concentrations at different times to be calculated from kinetic data.

The half-life is the time required for a reactant concentration to decrease to half its initial value. Its dependence on initial concentration varies with reaction order; for a first-order reaction, the half-life is independent of initial concentration.

topics.topic: Effect of temperature on reaction rate
topics.brief: Increasing temperature usually increases reaction rate because a greater fraction of molecules has enough energy to overcome the activation barrier. The size of the effect depends on the reaction's activation energy.
The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant to temperature and activation energy. It is commonly used to estimate activation energy from rate constants measured at different temperatures.

Activation energy is the energy barrier that reactants must overcome to reach the transition state along a reaction pathway. A catalyst can provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
Collision theory explains reaction rates in terms of collisions between reacting particles. Only collisions with sufficient energy and suitable orientation are effective in producing reaction.

A catalyst changes the reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway and is regenerated during the overall process. It does not change the equilibrium constant, although it helps the system reach equilibrium faster.

Homogeneous catalysis occurs when the catalyst and reactants are in the same phase, while heterogeneous catalysis involves different phases. In heterogeneous catalysis, reactions commonly occur at the catalyst's surface.

A reaction mechanism is a proposed sequence of elementary steps describing how reactants are converted into products. A valid mechanism must be consistent with the overall reaction and available kinetic and experimental evidence.

The rate-determining step is a sufficiently slow step that strongly influences the overall rate in a proposed reaction mechanism. Predicting the rate law may also require considering preceding equilibria and the details of the mechanism.
A thermodynamic system is the part of the universe selected for study, while the surroundings include everything outside it. Energy and matter may cross the boundary depending on the type of system.
An open system exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter, while an isolated system ideally exchanges neither matter nor energy.

State functions depend only on the current state of a system, not on how it reached that state. Internal energy, enthalpy, and entropy are state functions, whereas heat and work depend on the process pathway.
Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy associated with the particles of a system. Its change depends on the heat transferred to the system and the work done on it.

Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, while work is energy transferred through other organised interactions, such as expansion against an external pressure. Both are process quantities rather than state functions.

The first law expresses conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed. Using the chemistry sign convention, the internal energy change is commonly written as ΔU = q + w, where q is heat added and w is work done on the system.

Enthalpy is a thermodynamic state function defined as internal energy plus pressure multiplied by volume. At constant pressure, the enthalpy change equals the heat transferred when only pressure-volume work occurs.

The enthalpy change of a reaction is the difference between the enthalpies of products and reactants under the stated conditions. Exothermic reactions have negative enthalpy changes, while endothermic reactions have positive enthalpy changes.

Standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its constituent elements in their reference states under standard conditions. Elements in their reference states have a standard enthalpy of formation of zero.

Standard enthalpy of combustion is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions. It is usually negative because combustion reactions release heat.

Enthalpy of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when an acid and a base react to form one mole of water under specified conditions. Strong acid-strong base reactions in dilute aqueous solution have similar values because their net ionic reaction is the formation of water from H⁺ and OH⁻.

Hess's law states that the overall enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the pathway, provided the initial and final states are the same. It allows unknown enthalpy changes to be calculated from known thermochemical equations.

Bond enthalpy is the energy required to break a specified covalent bond in the gas phase. Average bond enthalpies can be used to estimate reaction enthalpy by comparing bonds broken with bonds formed.

Entropy is a state function related to the dispersal of energy and the number of accessible microscopic arrangements of a system. For an isolated system, spontaneous processes proceed in the direction of increasing total entropy.
The second law states that the total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease during a spontaneous process. It provides a criterion for the direction and spontaneity of thermodynamic changes.

Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy and is defined as G = H − TS. At constant temperature and pressure, a negative Gibbs free energy change indicates a thermodynamically spontaneous process in the forward direction.

A spontaneous process is thermodynamically favourable under the specified conditions, while a non-spontaneous process requires external driving or coupling to proceed in that direction. Spontaneity does not indicate how fast a process occurs.

topics.topic: Relationship between Gibbs energy and equilibrium
topics.brief: Gibbs energy is related to the reaction quotient and equilibrium constant. At equilibrium under specified conditions, the reaction Gibbs energy is zero, and the standard Gibbs energy change is related to the equilibrium constant through a logarithmic relationship.

Thermodynamic calculations use quantities such as enthalpy, entropy, internal energy, and Gibbs energy to analyse reactions and physical changes. Correct sign conventions, units, standard states, and balanced equations are essential for reliable results.

topics.topic: Oxidation and reduction in electrochemical systems
topics.brief: Oxidation involves loss of electrons, while reduction involves gain of electrons. Electrochemical systems couple these processes so that electron transfer can produce electrical energy or be driven by an external power supply.

An electrochemical cell uses oxidation-reduction reactions to convert chemical energy into electrical energy or electrical energy into chemical change. Its operation involves electrodes, an electrolyte, and a path for charge transfer.

A galvanic or voltaic cell produces electrical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction. Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, with electrons travelling through the external circuit from anode to cathode.

An electrolytic cell uses an external electrical supply to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction. It is used in processes such as electroplating, metal extraction, and the electrolysis of molten salts or aqueous solutions.

The anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs, and the cathode is where reduction occurs. The anode is negative in a galvanic cell and positive in an electrolytic cell; the cathode has the opposite sign in each type.

Cell notation is a compact representation of an electrochemical cell showing electrodes, phases, and the boundary between half-cells. A single vertical line usually represents a phase boundary, while a double vertical line represents a salt bridge or liquid junction.

Electrode potential describes the tendency of an electrode half-reaction to undergo reduction or oxidation relative to a reference electrode. Absolute electrode potentials are not measured directly; they are determined relative to a reference.

Standard electrode potential is the electrode potential measured under standard conditions relative to the standard hydrogen electrode. Standard reduction potentials help compare oxidising and reducing tendencies and calculate standard cell potentials.

The standard hydrogen electrode is a reference electrode involving hydrogen gas, hydrogen ions, and a platinum surface under specified standard conditions. Its standard electrode potential is assigned a value of zero volts.

The electrochemical series arranges redox couples according to their standard electrode potentials. It helps predict the direction of redox reactions, compare oxidising and reducing agents, and estimate cell potentials.

Cell potential is the electrical potential difference between the cathode and anode. Under standard conditions, the cell potential is calculated by subtracting the anode's standard reduction potential from the cathode's standard reduction potential.

The Nernst equation relates electrode or cell potential to the standard potential, temperature, and reaction composition. It is used to calculate cell potentials when conditions differ from standard conditions.

topics.topic: Relationship between cell potential and Gibbs energy
topics.brief: The Gibbs energy change of an electrochemical reaction is related to cell potential and the number of electrons transferred. A positive cell potential for the reaction as written corresponds to a negative Gibbs energy change under the same conditions.

topics.topic: Relationship between cell potential and equilibrium constant
topics.brief: The standard cell potential is related to the equilibrium constant through the standard Gibbs energy change. A large positive standard cell potential for the forward reaction corresponds to a large equilibrium constant at the specified temperature.

Conductance measures how readily an electrical current passes through a particular sample, while conductivity is a material property that accounts for the sample's dimensions. Ionic conductivity depends on the concentration, charge, and mobility of ions.

Molar conductivity is the conductivity contribution associated with one mole of electrolyte in solution. It depends on concentration and generally increases upon dilution, particularly for weak electrolytes as their ionisation increases.

Specific conductivity often decreases upon dilution because fewer ions are present per unit volume. Molar conductivity generally increases upon dilution as ionic interactions decrease and, for weak electrolytes, the degree of ionisation increases.

Kohlrausch's law of independent ionic migration states that at infinite dilution, each ion makes an independent contribution to the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte. It is useful for estimating limiting conductivities and certain weak-electrolyte properties.

Faraday's first law states that the amount of substance produced during electrolysis is proportional to the electric charge passed. The second law relates the amounts of different substances produced by the same charge to their chemical equivalent masses.

Electrolysis calculations relate electric current, time, total charge, and the amount of substance deposited or released. Faraday's constant and the electron stoichiometry of the electrode reaction are used to convert charge into moles of product.

Batteries store chemical energy and convert it into electrical energy through redox reactions. Fuel cells continuously generate electricity while fuel and oxidant are supplied, with performance and environmental impacts depending on their chemistry and energy sources.

Corrosion is the deterioration of a material through chemical or electrochemical reactions with its environment. It can be reduced through coatings, alloying, inhibitors, cathodic protection, and appropriate material selection.

Transition elements are commonly defined as elements whose atoms or cations have an incomplete d subshell. This definition explains many characteristic properties, although the classification of some Group 12 elements depends on the convention used.

Transition elements generally involve the filling of d orbitals, with configurations that may include partially filled d subshells. Some elements show exceptions to simple filling patterns because different orbital arrangements have similar energies.

Transition metals often exhibit variable oxidation states, coloured ions, complex formation, catalytic activity, and magnetic behaviour. Many also have high densities, high melting points, and the ability to form alloys.

Transition metals often exhibit multiple oxidation states because the energies of their outer s and d electrons are relatively similar. Different oxidation states can produce compounds with distinct colours, reactivities, and stability.

Many transition-metal ions form coloured compounds because electronic transitions can absorb portions of visible light. Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the surrounding ligands, and the geometry of the complex.

The magnetic behaviour of transition-metal species depends largely on the presence and arrangement of unpaired electrons. Species with unpaired electrons are generally paramagnetic, whereas species with all electrons paired are generally diamagnetic.

Transition metals and their compounds often act as catalysts because they can provide alternative reaction pathways, adsorb reactants, and change oxidation states. Their catalytic activity is important in industrial processes and biological systems.

Transition-metal ions form coordination complexes by accepting electron pairs from ligands. Their relatively small size, charge, and availability of suitable orbitals help them form complexes with characteristic structures and properties.

Transition metals readily form alloys with one another and with other elements. Alloying can alter strength, hardness, corrosion resistance, magnetic behaviour, and other physical or chemical properties.

Interstitial compounds form when small atoms, such as carbon, nitrogen, or hydrogen, occupy spaces within a metal lattice. These compounds may be hard, have high melting points, and retain some metallic conductivity.

topics.topic: Trends in atomic and ionic radii
topics.brief: Across a transition series, atomic and ionic radii often change only modestly because increasing nuclear charge is partly offset by shielding from d electrons. The precise trend depends on the series, oxidation state, and coordination environment.

Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion. Transition-metal ionisation energies show trends influenced by nuclear charge, electron configuration, and the relative energies of s and d orbitals.

The range and stability of oxidation states vary across a transition series because the availability and energies of d and s electrons change. Higher oxidation states are often stabilised by electronegative elements such as oxygen and fluorine.

Transition metals form many useful oxides, salts, complexes, and coordination compounds. Examples include potassium permanganate as an oxidising agent and compounds of iron, copper, nickel, and chromium used in industry and technology.

Transition metals are used in construction, electrical equipment, catalysts, pigments, batteries, and industrial machinery. Iron is important in steel production, copper in electrical wiring, and platinum-group metals in catalytic applications.

topics.topic: Definition and characteristics of heavy metals
topics.brief: Heavy metals is a broad term often used for metals with relatively high density, although definitions vary by scientific context. Some metals in this category are biologically essential in small quantities, while others can be toxic even at relatively low exposure levels.

Heavy metals occur naturally in rocks, minerals, soils, water, and living organisms. Mining, smelting, industrial activity, waste disposal, and some agricultural practices can increase their environmental concentrations.

Metal extraction separates a desired metal from its ore through processes such as concentration, roasting, reduction, leaching, or electrolysis. Refining then removes impurities to achieve the purity required for the intended application.

Iron forms common oxidation states of +2 and +3 and produces compounds such as iron(II) sulphate, iron(III) chloride, and iron oxides. Its chemistry is important in steel production, catalysis, biological systems, and water treatment.

Copper commonly forms +1 and +2 oxidation states and compounds such as copper(II) sulphate and copper oxides. Copper compounds are used in agriculture, electrochemistry, pigments, and industrial chemical processes.

Zinc usually forms the +2 oxidation state and compounds such as zinc oxide, zinc sulphate, and zinc chloride. Zinc is used for galvanising steel, manufacturing alloys, producing chemicals, and supporting essential biological functions.

Lead commonly forms +2 and +4 oxidation states, with lead(II) compounds being particularly common. Lead compounds have had industrial uses, but lead is toxic and its use is restricted in many applications because of health and environmental risks.

Mercury is a dense metal that is liquid near room temperature and forms compounds in several oxidation states, especially +1 and +2. Mercury and many of its compounds are toxic, and exposure can damage the nervous system and other organs.

Chromium commonly exhibits +3 and +6 oxidation states. Chromium(III) compounds have important industrial uses, whereas many chromium(VI) compounds are highly toxic and carcinogenic, requiring strict controls on handling and disposal.

Manganese exhibits several oxidation states, including +2, +4, and +7. Compounds such as manganese dioxide and potassium permanganate are used in batteries, oxidation reactions, water treatment, and chemical analysis.

The oxidation state of a metal describes its formal charge assignment within a compound and helps organise its redox chemistry. Different oxidation states influence solubility, colour, complex formation, and the oxidising or reducing behaviour of metal compounds.

Heavy-metal ions can bind to ligands such as water, ammonia, cyanide, or organic molecules to form coordination complexes. Complex formation influences metal solubility, mobility, reactivity, and biological availability.

Metals such as iron, copper, zinc, chromium, and manganese are used in alloys, construction, electrical systems, protective coatings, batteries, and chemical manufacturing. Their usefulness depends on their physical properties and chemical behaviour.

Some heavy metals can interfere with enzymes, damage cells, or accumulate in body tissues. Toxic effects depend on the specific element, chemical form, dose, exposure route, and duration; lead, mercury, and cadmium are important examples of hazardous metals.

Heavy-metal pollution occurs when metals accumulate in air, water, soil, or organisms at harmful concentrations. Sources include mining, industrial discharge, contaminated waste, and certain products, and some metals can persist and enter food chains.

Environmental monitoring measures metal concentrations in water, soil, air, and biological samples. Remediation techniques include stabilisation, soil washing, precipitation, adsorption, ion exchange, and selected biological methods, depending on the site and pollutant.

Non-metals generally have relatively high electronegativity and tend to gain or share electrons in chemical reactions. Their atomic size, ionisation energy, electron affinity, and reactivity vary systematically across periods and down groups.

Hydrogen is the lightest element and occurs in compounds such as water, acids, and hydrocarbons. Important hydrogen compounds include hydrides, hydrogen peroxide, and hydrogen halides, each with distinct bonding and chemical properties.

Oxygen is a reactive non-metal essential for respiration and combustion. Its compounds include oxides, peroxides, and oxygen-containing acids, while ozone is an allotrope with strong oxidising properties.

Nitrogen forms a wide range of compounds because of its ability to participate in covalent bonding and several oxidation states. Important examples include ammonia, nitric acid, nitrogen oxides, nitrates, and nitrites.

Phosphorus exists in several allotropes and forms compounds such as phosphine, phosphorus oxides, phosphoric acid, and phosphates. Phosphorus compounds are important in fertilisers, biological molecules, and industrial chemistry.

Sulphur occurs in several allotropes and forms compounds such as hydrogen sulphide, sulphur dioxide, sulphur trioxide, and sulphuric acid. These compounds have major industrial applications and can also contribute to environmental pollution.

Halogens are Group 17 elements that commonly form halide ions by gaining one electron. Their compounds include hydrogen halides, metal halides, interhalogen compounds, and oxyacids or oxyanions of some halogens.

Ammonia (NH₃) is a colourless gas with a pungent smell and weak basic properties in water. It can be prepared in the laboratory by heating an ammonium salt with a strong base and is manufactured industrially by the Haber process.

topics.topic: Preparation and properties of nitric acid
topics.brief: Nitric acid (HNO₃) is a strong acid and an oxidising agent. Industrially, it is produced by the Ostwald process, which involves catalytic oxidation of ammonia followed by conversion of nitrogen oxides into nitric acid.

topics.topic: Preparation and properties of sulphuric acid
topics.brief: Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) is a strong diprotic acid widely used in industrial manufacturing. It is produced by the Contact process and, when concentrated, acts as a dehydrating agent and can act as an oxidising agent.

Nitrogen forms several oxides, including nitrous oxide, nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and dinitrogen pentoxide. Their properties vary with oxidation state, and some nitrogen oxides contribute to acid rain, photochemical smog, and air pollution.

The principal oxides of sulphur are sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and sulphur trioxide (SO₃). They are important in sulphuric acid manufacture, and their release into the atmosphere can contribute to acid deposition and respiratory problems.

Hydrogen halides are covalent compounds such as HF, HCl, HBr, and HI. Their aqueous solutions form hydrohalic acids, and their acid strengths generally increase from HF to HI because the H-X bond becomes easier to break down the group.

Interhalogen compounds contain two different halogen elements, such as ClF, BrF₃, and IF₅. They are generally covalent and reactive, with molecular structures determined by bonding and electron-pair arrangements.

Oxyacids contain hydrogen, oxygen, and another central element. Examples include sulphuric acid, nitric acid, phosphoric acid, and chloric acids; their acidity depends on molecular structure, bond strengths, and the stability of their conjugate bases.

Non-metal compounds are used in fertilisers, medicines, food production, water treatment, chemical manufacturing, and energy technologies. Examples include ammonia for fertilisers, sulphuric acid in industry, and chlorine compounds for disinfection.

Some non-metal compounds contribute to air and water pollution, acid rain, greenhouse warming, or ozone-related environmental problems. The impact depends on the compound, its concentration, its persistence, and the conditions under which it is released.

Coordination compounds contain a central metal atom or ion bonded to surrounding ligands through coordinate bonds. They often have distinctive colours, magnetic properties, geometries, and chemical reactivities.

The central metal atom or ion is the species to which ligands attach in a coordination compound. It commonly accepts electron pairs from ligands and helps determine the complex's oxidation state, geometry, and properties.
Ligands are ions or molecules that donate one or more electron pairs to a central metal atom or ion. Examples include water, ammonia, chloride, and cyanide ions.

Coordination number is the number of donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal in a complex. It is not always equal to the number of ligand molecules because some ligands attach through multiple donor atoms.

The coordination sphere consists of the central metal and its directly attached ligands, usually written inside square brackets in a chemical formula. Ions outside the brackets balance the charge of the complex but are not directly coordinated to the metal.

topics.topic: Oxidation state of the central metal
topics.brief: The oxidation state of the central metal is calculated using the overall charge of the complex and the charges of its ligands. It helps determine the metal's electron configuration and can be used when naming coordination compounds.

Coordination nomenclature identifies ligands, their numbers, the central metal, and its oxidation state. The naming order and ligand names follow systematic rules, with anionic complexes generally using a modified metal name.

Ligands can be classified by charge, number of donor atoms, and bonding behaviour. Common categories include neutral ligands, anionic ligands, monodentate ligands, polydentate ligands, and bridging ligands.

Monodentate ligands bind to a metal through one donor atom, while polydentate ligands bind through two or more donor atoms. Polydentate ligands can form chelate rings and often produce especially stable complexes.

Chelation occurs when a multidentate ligand attaches to a metal ion through multiple donor atoms, forming one or more rings. Chelating agents are important in analytical chemistry, medicine, water treatment, and biological systems.

Coordination compounds can exhibit isomerism when they have the same overall composition but differ in connectivity or spatial arrangement. Main categories include structural isomerism and stereoisomerism.

Structural isomerism in coordination chemistry occurs when compounds differ in how ions or ligands are connected or distributed. Examples include ionisation, hydrate, linkage, and coordination isomerism.
Geometrical isomerism occurs when ligands occupy different relative positions around the same central metal. Cis-trans forms are common in square-planar and some octahedral complexes.

Optical isomerism occurs when coordination compounds form non-superimposable mirror-image structures called enantiomers. These isomers are often possible in complexes with suitable arrangements of multidentate ligands.

topics.topic: Basic ideas of valence bond theory
topics.brief: Valence bond theory describes coordination bonding through overlap between ligand donor orbitals and suitable orbitals associated with the central metal. It uses hybridisation models to explain common geometries, although it has limitations in predicting some spectral and magnetic properties.

The magnetic properties of coordination complexes depend on the number of unpaired electrons in the metal's d orbitals. Ligand strength, oxidation state, and geometry can influence whether electrons remain unpaired or pair up.

Coordination compounds are used in medicine, catalysis, metal extraction, analytical testing, pigments, and biological systems. Examples include metal-based drugs, haemoglobin, and complexes used to measure or separate metal ions.

Haloalkanes are compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms. They may be classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary according to the carbon attached to the halogen, and as mono-, di-, or polyhalogenated compounds.

Haloalkanes are named by selecting the longest carbon chain as the parent alkane and treating halogens as prefixes such as fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, or iodo-. Numbering gives substituents the lowest suitable locants under IUPAC rules.

Haloalkanes can be prepared by substitution of alkanes, addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes, or conversion of alcohols using suitable halogenating reagents. The method depends on the desired structure and reaction conditions.

Haloalkanes generally have higher boiling points than comparable alkanes because of their greater molar masses and intermolecular interactions. Their density and boiling point vary with the halogen, molecular size, and structure.

Carbon-halogen bonds are polar because halogens differ in electronegativity from carbon. This bond polarity influences reaction pathways, and the bond strength and leaving-group ability affect the reactivity of different haloalkanes.

Nucleophilic substitution occurs when a nucleophile replaces a leaving group, commonly a halide, attached to carbon. Haloalkanes can react through SN1 or SN2 mechanisms depending on their structure, solvent, nucleophile, and other conditions.

An SN1 reaction proceeds through a stepwise mechanism in which the leaving group departs first, often forming a carbocation, followed by nucleophilic attack. Its rate commonly depends on the concentration of the haloalkane alone.

An SN2 reaction occurs in a single concerted step in which the nucleophile attacks as the leaving group departs. It commonly involves backside attack and can cause inversion of configuration at a suitable chiral carbon.

Substitution reactions are influenced by substrate structure, nucleophile strength, solvent, leaving-group ability, and temperature. These factors determine whether an SN1 or SN2 pathway is favoured and how rapidly the reaction proceeds.

Elimination reactions remove atoms or groups from adjacent atoms, often forming a carbon-carbon double bond. Haloalkanes can undergo elimination when a base removes a hydrogen while the halide leaves.

Dehydrohalogenation removes a hydrogen atom and a halogen atom from a haloalkane to form an alkene. It commonly occurs with a suitable base, and product distribution depends on the substrate and reaction conditions.

Haloalkane reactivity depends on the reaction mechanism, carbon structure, and carbon-halogen bond. Tertiary substrates often favour SN1 reactions, while less hindered primary substrates commonly favour SN2 reactions with suitable nucleophiles.

Grignard reagents have the general formula RMgX and are prepared by reacting a suitable haloalkane with magnesium in dry ether or another suitable anhydrous solvent. Moisture must be excluded because it destroys the reagent.

Some halogenated compounds persist in the environment, contribute to ozone depletion, or present toxicity risks. The environmental impact varies substantially by compound, and many uses of ozone-depleting substances have been restricted or phased out.

Haloalkanes have been used as solvents, refrigerants, propellants, anaesthetics, and chemical intermediates. Some have significant toxicity or environmental impacts, so their use is governed by safety and environmental regulations.
Haloarenes are aromatic compounds in which a halogen is directly bonded to an aromatic ring. They are named by treating the halogen as a substituent, such as chlorobenzene or 1-bromo-2-methylbenzene.

Haloarenes can be prepared by direct halogenation of aromatic compounds using suitable catalysts or by reactions involving aromatic diazonium salts. The method depends on the halogen and the required aromatic product.

Haloarenes are generally poorly soluble in water and soluble in many organic solvents. Their boiling points, melting points, and densities depend on the halogen, molecular mass, and substitution pattern.

The carbon-halogen bond in haloarenes is stronger and has different bonding character from that in many haloalkanes. Interaction between the halogen lone pairs and the aromatic pi system gives the carbon-halogen bond partial double-bond character.

Resonance in haloarenes involves delocalisation of a halogen lone pair into the aromatic ring. This contributes to partial double-bond character in the carbon-halogen bond and helps explain why haloarenes are generally less reactive toward ordinary nucleophilic substitution than many haloalkanes.

Nucleophilic substitution in haloarenes is generally difficult under ordinary conditions but can occur with suitable activating groups or severe reaction conditions. Electron-withdrawing groups at appropriate positions can stabilise intermediates and facilitate substitution.

Haloarenes undergo electrophilic aromatic substitution because the aromatic ring retains its delocalised electron system. Halogens deactivate the ring overall but direct many incoming electrophiles toward the ortho and para positions.

Halogens withdraw electron density through the inductive effect, slowing electrophilic substitution, but donate electron density through resonance. The resonance contribution directs incoming electrophiles mainly to ortho and para positions.

Haloalkanes have halogens bonded to saturated carbon atoms, while haloarenes have halogens directly attached to aromatic rings. Their bond character, substitution mechanisms, and reactivities differ because of differences in bonding and electronic structure.

Haloarenes are used as intermediates in the production of pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, dyes, polymers, and other industrial chemicals. Some compounds require strict handling controls because of toxicity or persistence in the environment.

topics.topic: Environmental effects of halogenated aromatic compounds
topics.brief: Certain halogenated aromatic compounds persist in soil and sediments and may accumulate in organisms. Their environmental effects depend on structure, toxicity, persistence, and exposure, making careful control of industrial release and disposal important.

Alcohols contain a hydroxyl group (-OH) attached to a saturated carbon atom. They are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary according to how many carbon groups are attached to the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group.

Alcohols are named by selecting the longest chain containing the hydroxyl group and using the suffix '-ol'. The chain is numbered to give the hydroxyl group the lowest possible locant, and other substituents are named as prefixes.

Alcohols can be prepared by hydration of alkenes, hydrolysis of suitable haloalkanes, reduction of carbonyl compounds, or fermentation for certain alcohols. The appropriate method depends on the alcohol's structure and desired scale.

Alcohols can form hydrogen bonds, giving them relatively high boiling points compared with similar-sized hydrocarbons and ethers. Lower alcohols are generally miscible with water, while water solubility usually decreases as the hydrocarbon chain grows.
The hydroxyl group in alcohols allows intermolecular hydrogen bonding between molecules and with water. This interaction influences boiling point, viscosity, volatility, and solubility.

Alcohols are weak acids that can lose the proton from their hydroxyl group under suitable conditions. Their acidity depends on the stability of the resulting alkoxide ion and is generally weaker than that of water for many simple alcohols.
Alcohols react with sufficiently reactive metals such as sodium to form alkoxides and release hydrogen gas. The reaction demonstrates the weakly acidic character of the hydroxyl hydrogen.

Primary alcohols can be oxidised to aldehydes and further to carboxylic acids, while secondary alcohols generally form ketones. Tertiary alcohols resist ordinary oxidation because the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group lacks a hydrogen atom.

Dehydration removes water from an alcohol, often producing an alkene under acidic conditions and suitable heating. The product distribution depends on the alcohol's structure and the reaction conditions.

Alcohols react with hydrogen halides or related reagents to form haloalkanes by replacing the hydroxyl group with a halogen. Reaction rates and mechanisms depend on the alcohol structure and the reagent.
Esterification commonly involves the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to produce an ester and water. Acid catalysts and appropriate conditions help the reaction approach equilibrium.

topics.topic: Distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
topics.brief: Primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols can be distinguished by their structures and characteristic reactions. Oxidation behaviour and tests such as the Lucas test, when conducted under suitable conditions, can help differentiate these classes.

Methanol (CH₃OH) and ethanol (C₂H₅OH) are important simple alcohols used as solvents, fuels, and chemical feedstocks. Methanol is highly toxic, while ethanol can cause impairment and health harms when consumed excessively.

topics.topic: Industrial preparation and uses of alcohols
topics.brief: Alcohols are produced industrially through methods such as alkene hydration, synthesis from carbon monoxide and hydrogen for methanol, and fermentation for ethanol. They are used in solvents, fuels, pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, and chemical manufacture.

topics.topic: Health and safety aspects of alcohols
topics.brief: Alcohol hazards vary by compound and exposure route. Methanol can cause severe poisoning, ethanol is flammable and intoxicating, and many alcohols can irritate skin or eyes, so labels and safe handling practices must be followed.

Phenols contain a hydroxyl group directly attached to an aromatic ring. The simplest example is phenol, and substituted phenols are named by identifying the hydroxyl-bearing ring and numbering other substituents appropriately.

Phenols can be prepared by industrial processes involving cumene oxidation or by suitable reactions of aromatic compounds and their derivatives. The preparation method depends on the desired phenol and the available starting materials.

Phenols can form hydrogen bonds and often have higher boiling points than comparable aromatic hydrocarbons. Their solubility in water is limited but greater than that of many similarly sized non-polar aromatic compounds.

Phenols are weak acids that can donate a proton from the hydroxyl group to form phenoxide ions. The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance, which makes phenols more acidic than typical aliphatic alcohols.

topics.topic: Comparison of acidity of phenols and alcohols
topics.brief: Phenols are generally more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide conjugate base is stabilised by resonance. Alkoxide ions formed from ordinary alcohols lack the same aromatic resonance stabilisation.

Phenol reacts with active metals such as sodium to release hydrogen and form phenoxide salts. It also reacts with sufficiently strong bases such as sodium hydroxide, whereas ordinary alcohols generally do not react with aqueous sodium hydroxide to the same extent.

The hydroxyl group activates the aromatic ring toward electrophilic substitution by donating electron density through resonance. Substitution commonly occurs at the ortho and para positions relative to the hydroxyl group.
Phenol undergoes halogenation readily because its hydroxyl group activates the aromatic ring. The products and extent of substitution depend on the halogen, solvent, and reaction conditions.

Nitration introduces a nitro group into the aromatic ring of phenol. Because the hydroxyl group is activating and ortho-para directing, the products commonly include ortho- and para-substituted nitrophenols, depending on the conditions.
Sulphonation introduces a sulphonic acid group into the aromatic ring of phenol. The position of substitution can depend on the temperature and reaction conditions.

In the Kolbe-Schmitt reaction, sodium phenoxide reacts with carbon dioxide under suitable pressure and temperature, followed by acidification, to produce a hydroxybenzoic acid, commonly salicylic acid.

The Reimer-Tiemann reaction introduces a formyl group into phenol using chloroform and a strong base under suitable conditions. The major product is commonly 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde, also called salicylaldehyde.

Phenols are used in manufacturing resins, plastics, pharmaceuticals, dyes, and other chemical products. Some phenolic compounds also have antiseptic properties, although their safe use depends on the compound and concentration.

Phenol and many substituted phenols can be corrosive, toxic, or harmful to aquatic organisms. Exposure control, appropriate protective equipment, and safe disposal are important when handling these substances.
Ethers contain an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon-containing groups, with the general structure R-O-R'. They may be symmetrical, with identical groups, or unsymmetrical, with different groups.

In IUPAC nomenclature, many ethers are named as alkoxyalkanes, treating the smaller group attached through oxygen as an alkoxy substituent. Common names often list the two groups followed by the word 'ether'.

Ethers can be prepared by dehydration of suitable alcohols or by reactions that combine an alkoxide ion with an appropriate organic halide. The preferred method depends on the structure of the desired ether.

Williamson ether synthesis involves the reaction of an alkoxide ion with a suitable primary alkyl halide through an SN2 mechanism. It is an important method for preparing symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers.

Ethers are moderately polar but cannot donate hydrogen bonds to themselves because they lack an O-H bond. Their boiling points are generally lower than those of comparable alcohols, and smaller ethers have some solubility in water.

Ethers are relatively unreactive under many ordinary conditions but can react with strong acids and certain oxidising agents. Some ethers form explosive peroxides during prolonged exposure to air and light.

topics.topic: Cleavage of ethers by hydrogen halides
topics.brief: Strong hydrogen halides, especially HI and HBr, can cleave ether bonds under suitable conditions to produce alcohols and/or haloalkanes. The products depend on the ether structure, reagent amount, and reaction conditions.

Alcohols contain an O-H bond and can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while ethers can accept but not donate conventional hydrogen bonds. This difference affects boiling points, water solubility, acidity, and characteristic reactions.

Important ethers include diethyl ether, dimethyl ether, and cyclic ethers such as tetrahydrofuran. They have uses as solvents, chemical intermediates, and, in selected cases, fuels or aerosol propellants.

Ethers are used as solvents, extraction media, chemical intermediates, and components of some fuels. Their suitability depends on volatility, solvent properties, chemical stability, and safety considerations.

Many ethers are highly flammable, and some can form shock-sensitive explosive peroxides during storage. They should be handled away from ignition sources and stored and tested according to appropriate laboratory safety procedures.
The carbonyl group consists of a carbon atom double-bonded to oxygen. It is polar because oxygen attracts electron density, making the carbonyl carbon susceptible to attack by nucleophiles.

Aldehydes contain a terminal -CHO group, while ketones contain a carbonyl group bonded to two carbon-containing groups. IUPAC names commonly use the suffixes '-al' for aldehydes and '-one' for ketones.

Aldehydes can be prepared by controlled oxidation of primary alcohols or by other suitable synthetic routes. Reaction conditions are selected to limit further oxidation to carboxylic acids when the aldehyde is the desired product.
Ketones are commonly prepared by oxidation of secondary alcohols. Other methods include selected reactions of acid derivatives and transformations of suitable unsaturated or organometallic compounds.

topics.topic: Physical properties of aldehydes and ketones
topics.brief: The polar carbonyl group gives aldehydes and ketones dipole-dipole interactions. Their boiling points are generally higher than those of comparable non-polar hydrocarbons but lower than those of alcohols capable of intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

Oxygen attracts electron density from the carbonyl carbon, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and carbon a partial positive charge. This polarity explains the characteristic nucleophilic addition reactions of aldehydes and ketones.

Nucleophilic addition occurs when a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon and the pi bond shifts toward oxygen. Subsequent proton transfer or other steps produce the final addition product.
Aldehydes are readily oxidised to carboxylic acids or their corresponding carboxylates under suitable conditions. This behaviour forms the basis of tests such as Tollens' test and Fehling's test.

Reduction of aldehydes produces primary alcohols, while reduction of ketones produces secondary alcohols. Common reducing agents include sodium borohydride and lithium aluminium hydride, used under suitable conditions.

Aldol condensation involves aldehydes or ketones with suitable alpha hydrogens forming beta-hydroxy carbonyl compounds under acid or base catalysis. Further dehydration can produce alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compounds.

The Cannizzaro reaction occurs with certain aldehydes that lack alpha hydrogens in the presence of strong base. Two aldehyde molecules undergo disproportionation, producing an alcohol and a carboxylate salt.

Hydrogen cyanide can add across the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins. This reaction introduces a carbon-nitrogen bond and can be useful in organic synthesis, but cyanide reagents are highly toxic.

Aldehydes and ketones react with hydroxylamine to form oximes through a condensation reaction. Oxime formation is useful for identifying carbonyl compounds and preparing intermediates for further reactions.

Aldehydes and ketones react with hydrazine and related compounds to form hydrazones or other nitrogen-containing derivatives. These reactions are used in characterisation and in certain organic transformations.
Tollens' test uses an ammoniacal silver(I) reagent to detect many aldehydes. A positive result commonly produces a silver mirror or dark silver deposit as silver ions are reduced.
Fehling's test uses an alkaline copper(II) complex to detect many aliphatic aldehydes and reducing compounds. A positive result commonly produces a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.

The iodoform test detects compounds containing a suitable CH₃CO- group or those oxidisable to it under the test conditions. A positive result produces a pale yellow precipitate of triiodomethane, CHI₃.

Aldehydes are generally more readily oxidised than ketones and often give positive Tollens' or Fehling's tests. Most simple ketones do not give these results, although specific ketones can respond to other characteristic tests.

topics.topic: Uses of important aldehydes and ketones
topics.brief: Aldehydes and ketones are used in solvents, fragrances, resins, pharmaceuticals, food-related flavour compounds, and chemical manufacturing. Examples include formaldehyde in resin production and acetone as a widely used solvent.

topics.topic: Structure and nomenclature of carboxylic acids
topics.brief: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group (-COOH), which combines a carbonyl and a hydroxyl group on the same carbon. Their IUPAC names commonly use the suffix '-oic acid'.

Carboxylic acids can be prepared by oxidation of suitable primary alcohols or aldehydes, hydrolysis of nitriles, and reactions of organometallic compounds with carbon dioxide followed by acidification. The method depends on the required structure.

Carboxylic acids are polar and can form strong hydrogen-bonding interactions, often including dimers. Lower members are generally water-soluble, while solubility usually decreases as the non-polar carbon chain becomes longer.
Carboxylic acids donate a proton to form carboxylate ions. The conjugate base is stabilised by resonance across the two oxygen atoms, making carboxylic acids more acidic than ordinary alcohols.

Carboxylic acid strength depends on the stability of the carboxylate conjugate base. Electron-withdrawing groups generally increase acidity by stabilising negative charge, while electron-donating groups generally reduce acidity.
Carboxylic acids react with sufficiently reactive metals such as sodium to form carboxylate salts and release hydrogen gas. This reaction demonstrates their acidic character.
Carboxylic acids react with bases such as sodium hydroxide to form carboxylate salts and water. They also react with carbonates or bicarbonates to release carbon dioxide gas.

Esterification commonly involves a carboxylic acid reacting with an alcohol to form an ester and water. Acid catalysis and suitable conditions help establish the equilibrium between reactants and products.
Acid chlorides can be prepared from carboxylic acids using suitable chlorinating reagents. They are reactive carboxylic acid derivatives that readily undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution.

Acid anhydrides contain two acyl groups linked by an oxygen atom. They can be prepared through dehydration or reactions of suitable acid derivatives and are useful intermediates for making esters and amides.

Amides contain a carbonyl group bonded to nitrogen. They can be prepared from reactive carboxylic acid derivatives such as acid chlorides or anhydrides and ammonia or amines; direct reaction of a carboxylic acid with an amine often initially forms a salt.

Decarboxylation removes carbon dioxide from a carboxyl-containing compound. Certain carboxylic acids and their salts undergo this reaction under heating or other suitable conditions, sometimes producing a compound with one fewer carbon atom.
Carboxylic acids can be reduced to primary alcohols using sufficiently strong reducing agents such as lithium aluminium hydride. The carbonyl carbon's oxidation state decreases during the conversion.

Carboxylic acid derivatives include acid chlorides, acid anhydrides, esters, and amides. Their reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution depends largely on the leaving group's ability and the electronic properties of the acyl compound.

Carboxylic acids are used in food production, pharmaceuticals, polymers, cleaning products, and industrial synthesis. Examples include acetic acid in vinegar, citric acid in foods, and terephthalic acid in polyester manufacture.

topics.topic: Structure and classification of nitro compounds
topics.brief: Nitro compounds contain a nitro group (-NO₂) bonded to carbon. They are classified as aliphatic or aromatic according to whether the nitro group is attached to an aliphatic carbon or an aromatic ring.

Nitro compounds are named using the prefix 'nitro-' together with the name of the parent hydrocarbon or aromatic compound. Numbering identifies the position of the nitro group and any other substituents.

Nitroalkanes can be prepared by selected nitration reactions involving suitable aliphatic compounds or by other synthetic methods. The conditions and starting materials influence the product distribution.

Nitroarenes are commonly prepared by nitration of aromatic compounds using a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulphuric acid. The reaction introduces a nitro group through electrophilic aromatic substitution.

Nitro compounds are often polar because of the nitro group's charge distribution. Their boiling points, solubility, and physical state depend on molecular size, structure, and the presence of other functional groups.

Reduction of nitro compounds can produce amines under suitable conditions. Common methods use catalytic hydrogenation or chemical reducing agents, and the exact procedure depends on the substrate and other functional groups present.
