Nitroalkanes exhibit chemical behaviour influenced by the electron-withdrawing nitro group. Compounds with alpha hydrogens may form nitronate species under basic conditions and can participate in reactions useful for carbon-carbon bond formation.

The nitro group strongly withdraws electron density from the benzene ring, making nitrobenzene less reactive toward electrophilic substitution than benzene. Further substitution is generally directed toward the meta position.

topics.topic: Directive influence of the nitro group
topics.brief: The nitro group is strongly deactivating and meta-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution. Its electron-withdrawing effects destabilise the intermediates associated with ortho and para attack relative to meta attack.

Nitro compounds are used as intermediates in the manufacture of dyes, pharmaceuticals, agricultural chemicals, and other organic products. Their applications depend on their chemical structure and reactivity.

Some nitro compounds are toxic, flammable, or chemically unstable, and certain compounds present serious explosive hazards. Safe storage, handling, transport, and disposal depend on the specific substance and its safety data.

Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by carbon-containing groups. They are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary according to how many such groups are attached to nitrogen.

Primary amines have one carbon-containing group attached to nitrogen, secondary amines have two, and tertiary amines have three. Their structures influence basicity, hydrogen bonding, solubility, and characteristic reactions.

Aliphatic amines have nitrogen attached to aliphatic carbon groups, while aromatic amines have nitrogen directly attached to an aromatic ring. Aromatic amines such as aniline generally differ in basicity and reactivity because the nitrogen lone pair can interact with the ring.
Amines can be named using the suffix '-amine' or the prefix 'amino-' depending on the principal functional group. Substituents attached to nitrogen are identified with N-locants in systematic names.

Amines can be prepared by reduction of nitro compounds, reduction of nitriles or amides, ammonolysis of suitable haloalkanes, and other synthetic methods. The selected route influences whether primary, secondary, or tertiary products are obtained.

Amines are polar compounds, and primary and secondary amines can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Lower-molecular-mass amines may be soluble in water, while solubility generally decreases as the hydrocarbon portion becomes larger.

Amines act as bases because the nitrogen atom has a lone pair that can accept a proton. Their basicity depends on electron availability, solvation, steric effects, and the stability of the resulting ammonium ion.

Amine basicity is influenced by inductive effects, resonance, solvent interactions, steric hindrance, and the stability of the conjugate acid. Aromatic amines are often less basic than comparable aliphatic amines because the nitrogen lone pair can be delocalised into the aromatic ring.
Amines react with acids to form ammonium salts through protonation of the nitrogen lone pair. Many of these salts are more water-soluble than the corresponding neutral amines.

Alkylation introduces an alkyl group onto the nitrogen atom of an amine, commonly by reaction with an alkylating reagent. Repeated alkylation may produce secondary or tertiary amines and, under suitable conditions, quaternary ammonium salts.
Acylation introduces an acyl group onto the nitrogen atom of a suitable amine, forming an amide. It is commonly carried out using acid chlorides or acid anhydrides.

The carbylamine reaction is a test for primary amines in which a primary amine reacts with chloroform and a strong base to produce an isocyanide with a strong, unpleasant odour. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give the same characteristic reaction.

The Hinsberg test uses benzenesulfonyl chloride under basic conditions to help distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary amines. Their different reaction products and solubility behaviour allow the classes to be differentiated.

Diazotisation converts a primary aromatic amine, such as aniline, into an aromatic diazonium salt using nitrous acid under cold conditions. Temperature control is important because many diazonium salts are unstable at higher temperatures.

Aromatic diazonium salts contain the diazonium group attached to an aromatic ring. They are useful intermediates because the diazonium group can be replaced by other groups through suitable reactions.

Azo coupling is a reaction in which an aromatic diazonium ion reacts with an activated aromatic compound to form an azo compound containing an -N=N- linkage. Many azo compounds are brightly coloured and are used as dyes.

Primary, secondary, and tertiary amines can be differentiated using tests such as the Hinsberg test and the carbylamine reaction. Their reactions with nitrous acid can also differ according to the amine class and whether the amine is aliphatic or aromatic.

Amines are used in pharmaceuticals, dyes, polymers, agricultural chemicals, and water-treatment chemicals. Their basicity and ability to form derivatives make them useful intermediates in organic synthesis.

Organometallic compounds contain at least one direct bond between a metal or metalloid and the carbon atom of an organic group. They are important reagents and catalysts in organic and industrial chemistry.

Carbon-metal bonds vary in polarity and reactivity depending on the metal and the organic group. Many organometallic reagents have strongly polar carbon-metal bonds, making the carbon atom behave as a nucleophilic centre.

Organometallic compounds can be classified by the metal involved, the nature of the carbon-metal bond, and their structures. Important groups include organomagnesium, organolithium, organozinc, and transition-metal organometallic compounds.
Grignard reagents are prepared by reacting an organic halide with magnesium in a dry ether solvent. Water and other proton donors must be excluded because they react with and destroy the reagent.
Grignard reagents are highly reactive carbon nucleophiles and strong bases. They react with water, alcohols, acids, and other proton donors, so they must be handled under dry conditions.

topics.topic: Reactions of Grignard reagents with water
topics.brief: Grignard reagents react with water by proton transfer, producing a hydrocarbon and a magnesium-containing product. This reaction explains why moisture must be excluded during their preparation and use.

Grignard reagents react with carbon dioxide to form a magnesium carboxylate intermediate. Acidic work-up converts this intermediate into a carboxylic acid, usually adding one carbon atom to the organic framework.

Grignard reagents add to the carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and ketones, forming carbon-carbon bonds. Acidic work-up then produces alcohols, with the product class depending on the starting carbonyl compound.

Organometallic reagents enable the formation of carbon-carbon bonds, allowing chemists to build larger and more complex organic molecules. They are widely used in the synthesis of alcohols, acids, and many pharmaceutical intermediates.

Organolithium compounds contain a carbon-lithium bond and are generally strong bases and powerful nucleophiles. They are widely used in organic synthesis but require careful handling because they can react vigorously with water and air.

Many organometallic compounds act as catalysts in processes such as hydrogenation, carbon-carbon coupling, and polymerisation. Their metal centres can bind reactants and facilitate transformations through controlled reaction pathways.

Some organometallic reagents are air-sensitive, moisture-sensitive, corrosive, pyrophoric, or strongly reactive. Their handling requires suitable training, dry equipment, appropriate protective measures, and substance-specific laboratory procedures.

Polymers are large molecules made from repeating structural units and can be natural or synthetic. They are important in materials such as plastics, fibres, rubber, coatings, and biological substances.

A monomer is a small molecule that can react with other molecules to form a polymer. A repeating unit is the structural segment repeated along the polymer chain and may differ in appearance from the original monomer.

Polymers can be classified by origin, structure, monomer type, polymerisation mechanism, and thermal behaviour. Common categories include natural and synthetic polymers, linear and cross-linked polymers, and addition and condensation polymers.

Natural polymers occur in living organisms or nature and include cellulose, starch, proteins, and natural rubber. Synthetic polymers are manufactured through chemical processes and include polyethylene, nylon, polyester, and PVC.

Addition polymerisation joins unsaturated monomers, commonly containing carbon-carbon double bonds, without necessarily releasing a small by-product molecule. Polyethylene and polypropylene are familiar examples.

Condensation polymerisation joins monomers containing suitable functional groups, often with the elimination of small molecules such as water or methanol. Nylon and many polyesters can be produced through condensation reactions.
Thermoplastics soften when heated and harden when cooled, allowing them to be reshaped repeatedly under suitable conditions. Examples include polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, and polystyrene.
Thermosetting polymers form extensive cross-linked networks during curing and generally cannot be remelted and reshaped like thermoplastics. Examples include Bakelite and many epoxy resins.

Elastomers are polymers that can undergo substantial reversible deformation and recover much of their original shape. Their elasticity is associated with flexible chains and an appropriate degree of cross-linking.

Polymer fibres are materials with long, elongated structures that provide useful tensile strength and flexibility. Examples include nylon, polyester, acrylic fibres, and natural fibres such as cellulose-based cotton.

Polyethylene is an addition polymer made from ethene and is widely used in packaging, containers, films, pipes, and insulation. Its properties depend on factors such as chain branching, density, and molecular mass.
Polypropylene is an addition polymer made from propene. It is lightweight, chemically resistant, and used in packaging, fibres, automotive parts, household products, and medical supplies.

Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is produced by polymerising vinyl chloride. It is used in pipes, cable insulation, flooring, and other products, and its flexibility depends partly on additives such as plasticisers.

Polystyrene is an addition polymer made from styrene. It is used in packaging, disposable items, insulation, and protective foam, although its persistence in the environment makes waste management important.

Nylon is a family of synthetic polyamides known for strength, abrasion resistance, and useful fibre-forming properties. Different nylon types are used in clothing, ropes, engineering components, and industrial materials.

Polyesters contain ester linkages in their polymer chains and include materials such as PET. They are used in textile fibres, bottles, films, and engineering materials because of their useful mechanical and chemical properties.

Bakelite is an early thermosetting phenol-formaldehyde resin that forms a rigid cross-linked structure. It has been used in electrical components, handles, switches, and other products requiring heat resistance and electrical insulation.

Natural rubber is an elastomer obtained mainly from the latex of rubber-producing plants. It consists largely of cis-1,4-polyisoprene and has high elasticity but can be sensitive to heat, oxygen, and certain chemicals.
Vulcanisation treats rubber, commonly with sulphur, to create cross-links between polymer chains. This improves elasticity, strength, durability, and resistance to heat and deformation.

Biodegradable polymers can be broken down by biological activity under suitable environmental conditions. Their breakdown rate depends on polymer structure, temperature, moisture, microorganisms, and the disposal environment.

Polymers are used in packaging, construction, transport, electronics, medicine, textiles, and household products. Their low density, versatility, durability, and ease of processing make them valuable in many applications.

Plastic waste can persist in the environment, harm wildlife, block drainage systems, and fragment into microplastics. Reducing unnecessary use, improving collection, reusing products, and managing waste appropriately can reduce these impacts.

Polymer recycling includes mechanical processes that reprocess plastic materials and chemical processes that break polymers into useful molecules or feedstocks. Recycling effectiveness depends on polymer type, contamination, collection systems, and economic factors.

chapters.chapterName: Chemistry in the Service of Mankind

topics.brief: Chemistry supports medicine through the discovery, design, manufacture, and analysis of drugs and diagnostic substances. It also contributes to medical materials, imaging agents, disinfectants, and methods for monitoring biological processes.

Pharmaceutical chemistry studies the design, synthesis, properties, and analysis of substances used as medicines. It connects molecular structure with biological activity, safety, stability, and drug formulation.
Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth. They do not treat viral infections, and inappropriate use can promote antimicrobial resistance.

Antiseptics reduce microorganisms on living tissue, while disinfectants are primarily used on non-living surfaces. Their effectiveness depends on the active chemical, concentration, contact time, and target organism.

Analgesics relieve pain, while antipyretics reduce fever. Some medicines perform both functions; their selection and use depend on the person's circumstances, the product instructions, and appropriate medical advice.

Agricultural chemistry studies the chemical processes and materials involved in crop production, soil fertility, pest control, and plant nutrition. It supports efficient agriculture while helping evaluate environmental effects.

Chemical fertilisers supply nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to support plant growth. Correct application improves productivity, while excessive or poorly timed use can cause nutrient runoff, eutrophication, and other environmental problems.

Pesticides control organisms considered pests, while herbicides specifically target unwanted plants. Their use can protect crops but must be managed carefully to reduce risks to people, beneficial organisms, and ecosystems.

Food chemistry studies the composition, properties, and reactions of substances in food during processing, storage, cooking, and digestion. It helps explain flavour, colour, texture, nutrient stability, and food quality.

Food preservatives slow spoilage caused by microorganisms or chemical reactions. Examples include certain organic acids and their salts, while traditional preservation methods such as drying, salting, and pickling also help extend shelf life.
Soaps and detergents are surfactants that help water remove grease and dirt. Soaps are usually fatty-acid salts, while synthetic detergents often retain cleaning effectiveness in hard water.

Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons refined into fuels and chemical feedstocks. Petrochemical industries use these feedstocks to produce plastics, synthetic fibres, solvents, detergents, and many other materials.

Industrial chemical processes convert raw materials into useful products through controlled chemical reactions and separation steps. Examples include ammonia synthesis, sulphuric acid manufacture, petroleum refining, and polymer production.

Water treatment removes physical, chemical, and biological contaminants to make water suitable for drinking or other uses. Methods may include coagulation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection, and specialised processes for dissolved contaminants.

Environmental chemistry examines chemical substances and reactions in air, water, soil, and living systems. It helps identify pollution sources, understand contaminant behaviour, and develop strategies to protect ecosystems and human health.

Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and waste. Its principles encourage safer reagents, efficient reactions, renewable feedstocks, energy savings, and improved resource use.

Renewable and sustainable chemical technologies aim to reduce dependence on finite resources and minimise environmental impacts. Examples include renewable feedstocks, biomass conversion, cleaner energy systems, recyclable materials, and more efficient catalytic processes.

Chemical safety involves identifying hazards, assessing risks, and using appropriate controls during chemical manufacture, transport, storage, and use. Labels, safety data sheets, protective equipment, and proper disposal procedures help prevent accidents and exposure.

topics.topic: Social and environmental impacts of chemical industries
topics.brief: Chemical industries provide medicines, fertilisers, fuels, materials, and employment, but they can also generate emissions, hazardous waste, and occupational risks. Responsible production, regulation, pollution control, and community engagement help reduce negative impacts.
